blocks.text:
#### Multi-document transactions

Multi-document transactions are available on replica sets since MongoDB 4.0 and on sharded clusters since 4.2. A transaction runs inside a client session and provides ACID semantics across documents, collections, databases and, on a sharded cluster, shards. The contract has four parts.

- **Atomicity.** All writes of the transaction become visible together at commit, or none becomes visible after an abort.
- **Isolation.** Reads inside the transaction use the snapshot read concern: a consistent snapshot taken at the start of the transaction. Writes of other clients committed after that point are not visible to it. This is snapshot isolation, comparable to PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ`.
- **Conflict handling.** The first writer to modify a document wins. If a second transaction (or a non-transactional write) attempts to modify a document that the first has modified, the second fails immediately with a `WriteConflict` error carrying the label `TransientTransactionError`. MongoDB does not queue the second writer behind the first the way PostgreSQL row locks do for plain `UPDATE` statements.
- **Durability.** The transaction commits with the write concern given to the transaction, and `w: "majority"` is the correct choice for data that must survive a failover.

Snapshot isolation is not serializability. Two concurrent transactions that read overlapping data and write different documents can both commit, which is the write skew anomaly described in the transactions part of this book. The remedy is the same as in a relational database: make both transactions write to a common guard document so that the conflict detector sees the overlap.

blocks.text:
#### Limits and costs

Transactions are deliberately bounded. The documented defaults for MongoDB 7.x and 8.x are listed below.

rows: A transaction older than this is aborted by a periodic cleanup.
A transaction waits at most 5 ms for a lock before aborting.
A large transaction is split over several oplog entries; each entry must fit the BSON limit.
A transaction that reads must use the primary and one member throughout.
A transaction that dirties too much cache aborts (write conflict or TransactionTooLargeForCache).
blocks.caption: Operational limits of multi-document transactions.

blocks.text:
Two practical consequences follow. A transaction should touch tens of documents, not millions, and it should never wait for a user or an external service. A bulk migration is written as many small independent batches, each idempotent, rather than one large transaction. An in-flight transaction also blocks DDL on the collections that it touches, and a pending DDL operation in turn makes new transactions on those collections wait, so index builds and `drop` commands belong outside peak hours.

#### Write concern

Write concern defines when the server acknowledges a write. It has three fields: `w` (how many members must have applied the write), `j` (whether the members counted by `w` must have flushed the journal) and `wtimeout` (how long the primary waits for `w` before reporting a write concern error, which does not undo the write).

a majority of voting members have durably written the oplog entry

blocks.text: Since MongoDB 5.0 the implicit default write concern is `w: "majority"` for most deployments. The exception concerns arbiters: when the replica set has an arbiter and the number of data-bearing voting members does not exceed the voting majority (for example primary, one secondary and one arbiter), the implicit default is `w: 1`. With `w: "majority"` the journal flag defaults to true through `writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault`, so an acknowledged majority write is on disk on a majority of members. In MongoDB 8.0 and later a majority acknowledgement is sent once a majority has durably written the oplog entry; members apply the change asynchronously, so a secondary read immediately afterwards can still miss the write unless a causally consistent session is used.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A topology of one primary, one secondary and one arbiter has two data-bearing members. A majority write needs both data-bearing members; when either is down, every `w: "majority"` write blocks (or times out with `wtimeout`). Production replica sets use three data-bearing members instead of an arbiter.

#### Read concern and read preference

Read concern controls which version of the data a read may return; read preference controls which member serves the read.

rows: Returns the member's latest data; may later be rolled back after a failover. Default for reads outside transactions.
Like local; on a sharded cluster it may return orphaned documents. Lowest latency.
Returns only data acknowledged by a majority; it cannot be rolled back.
Single-document reads on the primary that reflect all majority-acknowledged writes completed before the read started; slow, requires a majority write concern for the writes.
A consistent point-in-time view; used inside multi-document transactions.
blocks.caption: Read concern levels.

blocks.text:
Read preference modes are `primary` (default), `primaryPreferred`, `secondary`, `secondaryPreferred` and `nearest`. Every mode except `primary` can return data that is behind the primary, because replication is asynchronous. The option `maxStalenessSeconds` (minimum 90 seconds) excludes secondaries whose estimated lag exceeds the given value, and tag sets restrict reads to members with given tags, for example one data centre. A replica set member that is briefly isolated can serve stale reads even with `primary` mode, until it steps down.

#### Causal consistency

A causally consistent session guarantees read your writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes follow reads, even when reads and writes go to different members. The driver records the `operationTime` of each write and sends it as `afterClusterTime` with later reads; the serving member waits until its data has reached that time. The guarantees hold only when the session uses read concern `majority` for reads and write concern `majority` for writes. Operations outside the session are not ordered with respect to it.

blocks.text:
#### Retryable writes and reads

A retryable write is retried exactly once by the driver after a transient network error or a replica set election, without applying the write twice. The driver attaches a session id and a transaction number to the command, and the server keeps a record of the outcome of each, so a repeated command returns the stored result. Drivers for MongoDB 4.2 and later enable retryable writes by default (`retryWrites=true`). Retryable operations are the single-document ones: `insertOne`, `insertMany`, `updateOne`, `replaceOne`, `deleteOne`, `findOneAndUpdate`, `findOneAndReplace`, `findOneAndDelete`, and `bulkWrite` consisting only of those. `updateMany` and `deleteMany` are not retryable, and neither is a write with `w: 0`. Commit and abort of a transaction are retryable. Retryable reads (`retryReads=true`) retry a read once in the same way.

### Worked example

The order service must create an order and reduce stock for each item. Stock lives in its own collection because it is updated by the warehouse system independently of orders, so the invariant spans two collections. The mongosh session below places order 1001 for two units of `A-100`. The statement `startTransaction` is local; no server round trip happens until the first operation. Typical output (not run on the build machine):

**Multi-document transaction in mongosh (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.code:
shop> const session = db.getMongo().startSession()
shop> session.startTransaction({ readConcern: { level: 'snapshot' },
...     writeConcern: { w: 'majority' } })
shop> const s = session.getDatabase('shop')
shop> s.orders.insertOne({ _id: 1001, customerId: 5434, status: 'NEW',
...   items: [{ sku: 'A-100', qty: 2 }] })
{ acknowledged: true, insertedId: 1001 }
shop> s.stock.updateOne({ sku: 'A-100', qty: { $gte: 2 } }, { $inc: { qty: -2 } })
{ acknowledged: true, insertedId: null, matchedCount: 1, modifiedCount: 1, upsertedCount: 0 }
shop> session.commitTransaction()
shop> session.endSession()

blocks.text:
Reading the sequence in order: the insert and the update execute inside the snapshot, and neither is visible to other clients until `commitTransaction`. The filter `qty: { $gte: 2 }` is the application-level invariant: when `matchedCount` is 0 the stock is insufficient and the code aborts instead of committing. If a second client had decremented the same `A-100` document after the snapshot was taken, the `updateOne` would have failed with a `WriteConflict` error labelled `TransientTransactionError`, and the whole transaction would have to be retried from `startTransaction`.

The same first-writer-wins behaviour can be reproduced for real on PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ`, which also uses snapshot isolation. Session A reads the stock row and sleeps; session B reads, updates and commits; session A then attempts its update. The output below was produced on the build machine (PostgreSQL 16).

blocks.code:
$ psql shop <<'EOF'   # session A, started first
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku='A-100';
SELECT pg_sleep(2);
UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE sku='A-100';
EOF
 qty
-----
  10
(1 row)

 pg_sleep
----------

(1 row)

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
blocks.title: First writer wins under snapshot isolation (PostgreSQL 16, real output)

blocks.text: Session B (not shown) ran `UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-2` and committed during the sleep, so the final quantity is 8 and the update of session A was rejected. MongoDB reports the same situation as `WriteConflict` and expects the application to retry; PostgreSQL reports SQLSTATE 40001. The difference is that PostgreSQL makes a later writer wait for the first one to finish before deciding, while MongoDB aborts the later writer at once.

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

#### Transaction code in Java with the callback API

The driver offers `ClientSession.withTransaction`, a callback API that starts the transaction, runs the body, commits, and automatically retries on `TransientTransactionError` and on `UnknownTransactionCommitResult` until a time limit of 120 seconds is reached. The listing uses the synchronous Java driver and is not run here because no driver jar is available on the build machine.

blocks.title: PlaceOrder.java (not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The body of the lambda can run more than once, therefore it must not have side effects outside the database (no emails, no messages). An exception thrown from the body aborts the transaction; `withTransaction` retries only the two labelled error types and rethrows everything else.

#### Observing write concern and read concern in mongosh

**Choosing durability per operation (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.text:
#### Write concern simulation of a failover

The effect of `w: 1` during a failover can be measured with a small model: one write per millisecond, an exponentially distributed replication delay (mean 12 ms) to each of two secondaries, a primary crash at 1.0 s, and the election of the more up-to-date secondary. Acknowledged writes that are absent from the new primary are counted as lost. The model is a simplification (no network partition, ordered oplog application, instant election), run on the build machine with a fixed random seed.

blocks.code:
$ python3 wc_sim.py
w1        acknowledged= 2002000 lost= 58224 failovers with loss=2000/2000 mean lost=29.11
majority  acknowledged= 1943521 lost=     0 failovers with loss=   0/2000 mean lost=0.00
blocks.title: Failover loss simulation (real output of the model, 2000 failovers)

blocks.text: The result is structural and not an artefact of the parameters: with `w: 1` the client is told "done" at the moment the primary applies the write, so every write that has not yet reached a secondary when the primary fails is acknowledged and then lost. With `w: "majority"` the acknowledgement is delayed until a secondary has the write, so the number of acknowledged writes is slightly lower (about 29 writes per failover were still in flight and are reported as errors, to be retried by the client), and none of the acknowledged ones disappears.

blocks.text:
### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: stale reads from a secondary

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot service reads orders with `readPreference=secondaryPreferred` to offload the primary. After a status update, a customer reloads the order page and still sees the previous status.

**Symptoms.** Support tickets state that "the status did not change". The write is present when checked in mongosh against the primary. The effect is intermittent and worse during imports and backups.

**Diagnosis.** In order:

1. Confirm that the read was served by a secondary: the connection string or `@ReadPreference` setting, or `db.currentOp()` on the secondaries.
2. Measure replication lag. Typical output (not run on the build machine):

**Replication lag per secondary (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

1. Check whether the lag correlates with load: `db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.concurrentTransactions` (or `queues.execution` on 7.0 and later), oplog window in `rs.printReplicationInfo()`, and disk latency on the secondary.

**Root cause.** Replication is asynchronous, so a secondary always shows a past state. The service issues a write to the primary and an immediate read to a secondary with no ordering between them.

**Fix.** Immediate: route the read-after-write path to the primary (`primaryPreferred` or `primary`). Permanent: use a causally consistent session with `majority` read and write concern for flows that must read their writes, and keep `secondaryPreferred` only for reads that tolerate lag, with `maxStalenessSeconds` set.

**Prevention.** Alert on replication lag above a threshold (for example 10 seconds); document which endpoints tolerate stale data; test read-after-write behaviour with an artificial delay on a secondary.

blocks.text:
#### Incident: wrong write concern loses acknowledged writes on failover

**Scenario.** A payment-event collection is written with `w: 1` (set explicitly in the connection string years ago to reduce latency). A maintenance window triggers a primary step-down during peak traffic.

**Symptoms.** After the failover the application reports no errors, but reconciliation finds events that the application logged as stored and that are missing in MongoDB. The old primary logs a rollback.

**Diagnosis.**

1. Search the log of the former primary for the rollback and for the saved files.

blocks.code:
$ grep -i "rollback" /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log | grep -i "files\|complete" | tail -3
{"t":{"$date":"2026-10-12T02:14:51.201+00:00"},"s":"I","c":"ROLLBACK","msg":"Rollback complete"}
$ ls /var/lib/mongodb/rollback/*/
removed.2026-10-12T02-14-50.0.bson
$ bsondump /var/lib/mongodb/rollback/*/removed.2026-10-12T02-14-50.0.bson | wc -l
37
blocks.title: Finding rolled-back data (typical output, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
1. Compare the effective write concern: the connection string, `db.adminCommand({getDefaultRWConcern: 1})`, and the per-operation options in the code.

**Root cause.** A `w: 1` write is acknowledged before replication. The old primary held 37 acknowledged writes that no secondary had received; the new primary never saw them, so on rejoining, the old primary rolled them back.

**Fix.** Immediate: recover the documents from the BSON files in the `rollback` directory (inspect with `bsondump`, reinsert after verification). Permanent: set `w=majority` in the connection string or `WriteConcern.MAJORITY` on the collection, and set the cluster default with `setDefaultRWConcern`.

**Prevention.** Keep write concern explicit in configuration; add a failover test (`rs.stepDown()` under load in staging) to the release checklist, and treat `w: 1` for business data as a defect.

#### Incident: multi-document transaction timeouts

**Scenario.** A nightly job closes expired orders in one transaction: it iterates 200,000 orders, updates each, and decrements counters. The job worked in testing with 2,000 orders.

**Symptoms.** The job fails with `NoSuchTransaction` or `TransactionExpired` after about 60 seconds; during the run, online order updates fail with `WriteConflict`.

**Diagnosis.**

1. `db.currentOp({ 'transaction': { $exists: true } })` shows the transaction age and its lock count; `db.serverStatus().transactions` shows `totalAborted` growing.
2. The log contains the abort reason (`transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds`).

**Root cause.** The transaction exceeds the 60-second lifetime and holds write locks on 200,000 documents, so every concurrent writer of those documents conflicts with it.

**Fix.** Immediate: run the job in batches of 500 documents, each in its own short transaction (or, when no cross-document invariant exists, with plain `updateMany` over a bounded batch). Permanent: keep an idempotent marker (`closedAt`) so that a failed batch is re-run safely. Raising `transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds` is not a fix: it extends lock holding and cache pressure.

**Prevention.** Load-test with production volumes; alert on `transactions.totalAborted`; keep transactions below tens of documents and a few seconds.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **Is a single MongoDB write atomic?** A write to one document is atomic including embedded documents and arrays. A write that spans several documents (`updateMany`) is atomic per document only; a multi-document transaction is needed for atomicity across documents.
2. **What isolation level do MongoDB transactions provide?** Snapshot isolation: reads see a consistent snapshot, conflicting writers abort with `WriteConflict` (first writer wins). It is not serializable, so write skew is possible.
3. **What does** `w: "majority"` **guarantee and what does it not?** The write has been durably written by a majority of voting members and will survive an election. It does not make the data visible on every secondary yet.
4. **When is** `w: 1` **acceptable?** For data that can be regenerated or is of little value (metrics, caches). Not for business records, because a failover can roll back acknowledged writes.
5. **What is the difference between read preference and read concern?** Read preference chooses the member; read concern chooses the consistency and durability level of the data returned. `secondary` with `majority` still returns possibly stale but never rolled-back data.
6. **How does a retryable write avoid a double insert?** The driver sends a session id and transaction number; the server records the result and returns it if the same pair is received again.
7. **Why can a transaction abort with** `TransientTransactionError` **and what does the application do?** A write conflict, a failover or a lock timeout aborted it. The application restarts the whole transaction; the callback API does this automatically.
8. **Why prefer embedding to multi-document transactions?** Embedding makes the invariant a single-document write: atomic, one round trip, no lock holding, no 60 second limit.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Single-document writes are atomic; model data so that invariants fit in one document.

- Multi-document transactions give snapshot isolation with first-writer-wins conflicts, a 60 second default limit and a 5 ms lock wait; keep them small and retry on `TransientTransactionError`.
- `w: "majority"` is required for acknowledged data to survive a failover; `w: 1` loses roughly the in-flight writes of every failover.
- Read preference selects the member, read concern the version of data; non-primary reads can be stale.
- Causal sessions with majority concerns give read your writes across members.
- Retryable writes cover single-document operations only.

A single mongod process is a single point of failure for availability and, until the disk is backed up, for data. MongoDB replicates data with replica sets: a group of mongod processes that hold copies of the same data and elect one member as primary to accept writes. Replication provides redundancy, automatic failover and the ability to serve reads, backups and analytics from additional members. It does not provide horizontal write scaling; that is the task of sharding. The chapter explains the mechanisms in enough depth to predict what happens during a failure and to size the settings that govern it.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Members and roles

A replica set has up to 50 members, of which at most 7 vote. One member is the primary; it is the only member that accepts writes. The other data-bearing members are secondaries that copy the primary's operations. Members can take special roles through configuration.

rows: Accepts writes and, by default, reads
Never becomes primary; used for a remote data centre or dedicated reads
Invisible to drivers; used for reporting and backups
Holds a state N seconds old; protection against logical errors

blocks.text:
An arbiter provides a vote without providing a copy of the data. It cannot acknowledge writes, so it reduces the availability of `w: "majority"` (see the previous chapter), and it prevents some operations such as changing a shard key in a transaction. The recommended deployment is three data-bearing members in three failure domains.

#### The oplog

The primary applies every write to its data and records it in the oplog, a capped collection named `local.oplog.rs`. Each entry has a timestamp `ts`, a term `t`, an operation type `op` (`i` insert, `u` update, `d` delete, `c` command, `n` no-op), the namespace `ns` and the operation `o`. Entries are idempotent: applying one twice yields the same state, which makes replication and recovery safe to repeat. A secondary fetches entries from its sync source (normally the primary, optionally another secondary, which is chained replication), writes them to its own oplog and applies them in batches.

The oplog is a fixed-size ring: when it is full, the oldest entries are overwritten. The interval covered by the oplog is the oplog window. A secondary that stays down longer than the window cannot catch up from the oplog and must perform an initial sync (full copy). The default size on WiredTiger is a percentage of free disk space with documented minimum and maximum bounds, and it can be changed online with `replSetResizeOplog`.

#### Elections

MongoDB uses a Raft-like protocol (replication protocol version 1). Time is divided into terms, each beginning with an election. Members exchange heartbeats every 2 seconds. A secondary that has not heard from the primary for `electionTimeoutMillis` (default 10 seconds) first runs a dry-run election to check that it would win, and then starts a real election with an incremented term. Each member votes at most once per term and refuses a candidate whose oplog is behind its own, so the winner holds the most recent majority-committed data. A candidate that gathers votes from a majority of voting members becomes primary. A primary that cannot reach a majority steps down on its own, which prevents two primaries from accepting writes that both survive.

blocks.text: Priority influences who is elected: a higher-priority member calls elections sooner and is favoured, but priority is not a guarantee. Use `priority`, not `votes`, to prefer a member. The MongoDB documentation gives a median time to elect a new primary of no more than 12 seconds with default settings. Lowering `electionTimeoutMillis` shortens detection but increases spurious elections and rollbacks of `w: 1` writes. Writes are unavailable between the loss of the primary and the election of its successor; reads from secondaries remain possible under a suitable read preference.

blocks.text:
#### Rollback

If the old primary had accepted writes that no member received before it lost its primacy, those writes are on the old primary only. When it rejoins as a secondary it finds that its oplog diverges from the new primary's. It finds the common point, reverts its data to that point and applies the new primary's entries. The reverted inserts and updates are written to BSON files under `dbpath/rollback/<collection UUID>/removed.<timestamp>.bson`; reverted deletes and drops are not saved. Rollback is rare and, for writes with `w: "majority"`, impossible by construction. A member whose divergence exceeds `rollbackTimeLimitSecs` (24 hours by default) cannot roll back and must be resynchronised.

blocks.text:
#### Flow control and initial sync

A new or stale member runs an initial sync: it clones all databases, applies the oplog that accumulated during the clone, and then switches to normal replication. Initial sync of a large dataset takes hours and competes for I/O with production traffic. Since MongoDB 4.2 a flow control mechanism throttles the primary's writes when the majority commit point lags more than a target (10 seconds by default), trading write throughput for bounded lag.

### Worked example

A replica set `rs0` has three members. The primary holds oplog position 107, secondary 1 position 106 and secondary 2 position 104. The question is which write is acknowledged to a `w: "majority"` client, which writes a `majority` reader sees, and what a failover would lose.

1. The majority of three voting members is two. The positions sorted are 107, 106, 104. The second highest position, 106, is present on at least two members: this is the majority commit point.
2. A write at position 106 or lower is acknowledged to a `w: "majority"` client. The write at 107 is acknowledged to a `w: 1` client already, but a `w: "majority"` client waits.
3. A `majority` reader sees the state up to position 106 only. Position 107 might still be rolled back.
4. If the primary now fails, secondary 1 (position 106) and secondary 2 (position 104) hold an election. Secondary 2 cannot win: the voter secondary 1 refuses a candidate with a shorter oplog. Secondary 1 wins and becomes primary at term 4. Entry 107 existed only on the old primary and is lost: it was acknowledged only to `w: 1` clients.
5. Secondary 2 catches up from the new primary (entries 105 and 106). When the old primary returns, it rolls back entry 107 to a file and resumes as a secondary.

The simulation in the previous chapter reproduces exactly this step 4 at scale: every acknowledged `w: 1` write beyond the surviving prefix is lost.

### Hands-on

#### Starting a three-member set and reading its status

The commands below create a development replica set on one machine (three mongod processes on different ports). They are shown for reference; MongoDB is not installed on the build machine, so the output is typical.

blocks.code:
$ mongod --replSet rs0 --port 27017 --dbpath /data/rs0-0 --bind_ip localhost \
    --fork --logpath /data/rs0-0.log
$ mongod --replSet rs0 --port 27018 --dbpath /data/rs0-1 --bind_ip localhost \
    --fork --logpath /data/rs0-1.log
$ mongod --replSet rs0 --port 27019 --dbpath /data/rs0-2 --bind_ip localhost \
    --fork --logpath /data/rs0-2.log
$ mongosh --port 27017 --eval 'rs.initiate({_id: "rs0", members: [ \
    {_id: 0, host: "localhost:27017"}, {_id: 1, host: "localhost:27018"}, \
    {_id: 2, host: "localhost:27019"}]})'
{ ok: 1 }

blocks.text:
#### Planned failover and configuration changes

**Step down and prefer a member (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

`rs.stepDown(60)` makes the primary ineligible for election for 60 seconds, so the failover is controlled and quick (the primary waits for an electable secondary to catch up first). Planned maintenance always uses `stepDown`, never `kill` of the primary.

#### Connection string for a replica set

blocks.code:
spring.data.mongodb.uri=mongodb://db1:27017,db2:27017,db3:27017/shop?replicaSet=rs0\
  &w=majority&readPreference=primary&retryWrites=true&retryReads=true
blocks.title: application.properties

blocks.text:
The driver discovers the members through the seed list, monitors them, and reroutes after an election. Listing all members in the seed list lets the driver connect even when one is down; the `replicaSet` name must match.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: failover causing write errors despite retryable writes

**Scenario.** A planned primary step-down is executed during business hours. The order service uses retryable writes and expects no visible errors.

**Symptoms.** For about 12 seconds the service logs `MongoNotPrimaryException` or `MongoSocketReadException`, and some HTTP requests fail with timeouts. A few `updateMany` batches fail outright.

**Diagnosis.**

1. Check which operations failed: single-document writes are retried once; `updateMany` and `deleteMany` are not retryable; a `w: 0` write is never retried.
2. Compare the client timeouts with the election time. `serverSelectionTimeoutMS` (default 30 seconds) bounds how long the driver waits for a primary; an HTTP timeout of 5 seconds is shorter than the election.
3. Review the log of the members for the election time: `"Starting an election"` and `"Election succeeded"` messages.

**Root cause.** Retryable writes retry once after the new primary is found, but the retry cannot start before the election completes (typically up to about 12 seconds). Non-retryable operations return the error to the caller, and short upstream timeouts convert the wait into failures.

**Fix.** Immediate: retry failed bulk operations in the application with backoff (they are safe when idempotent). Permanent: make bulk updates idempotent and retried by the caller; set HTTP and driver timeouts consistently (`timeoutMS` or `serverSelectionTimeoutMS` longer than the expected election); schedule `stepDown` for low-traffic periods.

**Prevention.** Run failover drills in staging with production-like load; track the error rate during each maintenance; expose the number of retries as a metric.

#### Incident: replica set unavailable for writes after losing one data centre

**Scenario.** A five-member replica set has two members in data centre A and three in data centre B. Data centre B loses power.

**Symptoms.** The two members in A remain up but are both secondaries; applications report `NotWritablePrimary`. **Diagnosis.** `rs.status()` shows the members in B as `(not reachable/healthy)`, and the members in A as `SECONDARY`. Two of five votes are not a majority.

**Root cause.** A majority of voting members (3 of 5) is required both to elect a primary and for `w: "majority"`. The majority lived in the failed site, so the surviving site cannot elect.

**Fix.** Immediate: when B cannot be restored, reconfigure A with `rs.reconfig(cfg, { force: true })` after confirming that B is permanently down (this can lose writes that only B held). Permanent: place members so that no single site holds a majority: for five voters use 2 + 2 + 1 across three sites.

**Prevention.** Design the topology from the failure it must survive; test by isolating a site in staging.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **How does MongoDB elect a primary?** A secondary that misses heartbeats for the election timeout (10 s default) runs a dry-run and then a real election in a higher term. Voters grant one vote per term and only to a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as their own. A majority wins.
2. **What is the oplog and why is it idempotent?** A capped collection of operations in `local.oplog.rs`. Each entry records the resulting change in a form that can be applied repeatedly with the same result, which makes replay after a crash or during initial sync safe.
3. **What is a rollback and how is it avoided?** A former primary reverts writes that no other member received. Using `w: "majority"` guarantees that acknowledged writes are not rolled back.
4. **Why are two data members plus an arbiter a poor design?** Majority writes require both data members; one failure blocks them and leaves only one copy. Three data-bearing members avoid both problems.
5. **What happens if a secondary is down longer than the oplog window?** It cannot resume from the oplog and needs a full initial sync.
6. **How do reads from secondaries relate to consistency?** They can be stale by the replication lag. Use causal sessions with majority concerns when a read must reflect a prior write.
7. **What do hidden and delayed members do?** Hidden members serve reporting and backups without receiving driver traffic. A delayed member keeps a historical state as protection against logical errors such as an accidental drop.
8. **How does the number of members affect fault tolerance?** The set tolerates the loss of a minority: 3 members tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. An even number adds no tolerance over the odd number below it.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A replica set elects one primary by majority vote; the oplog carries idempotent operations to secondaries.

- Election takes about 10 to 12 seconds with default settings; writes are unavailable during that time.
- Only `w: "majority"` writes are protected from rollback; rolled-back inserts and updates are saved as BSON files.
- Put voting members in at least three failure domains and avoid arbiters in new designs.
- Reads from secondaries are stale by the replication lag; bound it with `maxStalenessSeconds` or avoid it for read-after-write.

A replica set stores the complete dataset on every member and sends every write through one primary. When the dataset exceeds the storage or memory of one machine, or the write rate exceeds what one primary can apply, the data must be divided. Sharding partitions a collection across several replica sets (shards), each holding a subset of the documents. The application sees one logical collection; routing, balancing and metadata are handled by the cluster. The price is a design decision that is hard to reverse: the shard key. A poor shard key produces a hot shard, jumbo chunks or queries that touch every shard. This chapter covers the components, the criteria for a shard key, the mechanics of chunks and the balancer, query routing, zones and resharding. Experiments that the build machine could run (simulations of key distributions) are marked as such; cluster commands are typical output.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Components

A sharded cluster has three kinds of process.

- **Shards.** Each shard is a replica set that stores a subset of the sharded data (and the complete data of unsharded collections assigned to it as the primary shard of a database).
- **Config servers.** A replica set (CSRS) that stores the cluster metadata: the list of shards, the chunk map of each collection, zone definitions and the state of the balancer.
- **mongos routers.** Stateless processes that applications connect to. A mongos caches the chunk map, routes each operation to the shards that own the relevant data, and merges results. Several mongos instances are deployed for availability, commonly one per application host.

blocks.text:
#### The shard key

The shard key is one field or several fields of every document that determines the shard on which the document lives. It must be backed by an index (created automatically on an empty collection) and every document must have its value (missing fields are treated as null). Since MongoDB 4.2 the value of a shard key field can be modified, except `_id`, and since 4.4 the key can be refined by appending fields (`refineCollectionShardKey`); since 5.0 the whole key can be changed by resharding. A shard key is therefore no longer permanent, but changing it moves data and costs hours on a large collection.

Four properties determine the quality of a shard key.

1. **Cardinality.** The number of distinct values bounds the number of chunks. A key such as `country` with 200 values cannot spread beyond 200 chunks, and a key such as `status` with 5 values cannot spread at all.
2. **Frequency.** The distribution of the values matters as much as their number. When one value covers 55 percent of the documents, the chunk for that value cannot be split, because a split needs two different key values. Such a chunk is flagged jumbo.
3. **Monotonic change.** A key that grows with time (timestamp, `ObjectId`, auto-increment number) in a range-sharded collection directs all new inserts to the chunk that holds the maximum value, and therefore to a single shard. The balancer redistributes stored data but cannot redistribute the insert load.
4. **Query isolation.** The key should appear in the filters of the frequent queries. A query that contains the shard key (or a prefix of a compound key) is targeted at one shard or a few; a query without it is broadcast to all shards (scatter-gather).

A hashed shard key (`{ customerId: 'hashed' }`) applies a hash function to the value, which spreads monotonic and clustered values uniformly. The price is that range queries on the key become scatter-gather, because neighbouring values are on different shards. A ranged key keeps neighbours together, so range queries are targeted, at the risk of hot spots. Compound keys combine both: `{ region: 1, customerId: 'hashed' }` is supported since MongoDB 7.0, and a hashed field in the second position is the common pattern to spread within one region.

*Shard key candidates for the orders collection (100,000 documents in the experiment below).*

#### Chunks and the balancer

The range of shard key values is divided into chunks: contiguous ranges, each assigned to one shard. A chunk is a metadata concept; documents are not stored per chunk. The default maximum chunk size ("range size") is 128 MB. When a chunk grows beyond it, it is split at a median key value. The balancer, a process running on the config server primary, compares the data volume of each shard per collection and migrates ranges from the shard with the most data to the shard with the least when the difference exceeds three times the range size (384 MB with the default). Each shard takes part in one migration at a time, and a cluster with n shards runs at most n/2 migrations concurrently.

A migration copies the range to the recipient, forwards writes that occurred during the copy, briefly blocks writes to the range while the ownership is committed in the config metadata (the critical section), and then deletes the donor copy asynchronously. The balancer can be restricted to a window with `sh.setBalancerState` and the `balancerWindow` setting so that migrations do not compete with peak traffic.

blocks.text:
A chunk with too many documents to move (above roughly twice the range size divided by the average document size) or a single key value that cannot be split is a jumbo chunk. It remains on its shard, grows without bound and skews the cluster. Since MongoDB 6.0 the balancer balances by data size and splitting is performed lazily (when a chunk must be moved), which removed most automatic split work, but the jumbo condition itself still follows from the key.

#### Query routing

For a read or write, mongos extracts the shard key conditions from the filter and consults its chunk map. If the filter contains an equality on the full shard key, exactly one chunk is addressed. A range or `$in` on the shard key addresses the chunks that overlap. A filter without the leftmost shard key field is sent to every shard (scatter-gather), and mongos merges sorted partial results. Aggregation pipelines are split: stages that can run per shard (`$match`, `$project`, partial `$group`) run on the shards, and a merging stage runs on one shard or on mongos. Inserts need the full shard key in the document; updates and deletes that address a single document should include the shard key in the filter or use the `_id` together with it.

blocks.text:
Unique indexes on a sharded collection must include the shard key as a prefix, because each shard can enforce uniqueness only within its own data. A unique constraint on `email` therefore requires either shard key `{ email: 1 }` or a separate lookup collection keyed by email.

#### Zone sharding

Zones associate ranges of the shard key with a subset of shards. The balancer then places chunks of a range only on shards of the matching zone. The typical uses are data residency (European customers on European shards), tiered hardware (recent data on fast shards, old data on cheap shards) and isolating a tenant. The shard key must begin with the field that defines the zone.

blocks.text:
#### Resharding

`db.adminCommand({ reshardCollection: 'shop.orders', key: { customerId: 'hashed' } })` (MongoDB 5.0 and later) rebuilds the collection under a new key online: it copies the data to a new collection layout in the background, applies the changes that occur during the copy, and then switches over in a short critical section. It needs spare storage (a full copy), I/O and a window of low write traffic near the end, and it is the documented remedy for a shard key that proved wrong. MongoDB 8.0 added `moveCollection` and `unshardCollection` and a faster rebalance with the same key; 7.0 added `analyzeShardKey`, which samples queries and reports the cardinality, frequency and monotonicity of candidate keys before committing to them.

### Worked example

The orders collection receives 100,000 inserts distributed over four shards. The question is which shard key keeps the insert load even. The experiment is a simulation with a Python model of the chunk mechanism: chunks split at the median key when they exceed 1,000 documents (a scaled-down range size), a balancer moves chunks from the shard with most chunks to the one with fewest every 5,000 inserts, and each insert is routed to the shard that owns its chunk at that moment. Three keys are compared: a monotonic key (the insertion order, as `ObjectId` or a timestamp would give), the hash of `_id`, and a uniformly random key. The hash is MD5-based and stands in for the MongoDB hash function. Real output of the model:

blocks.code:
$ python3 shard_sim.py
key                    chunks  inserts per shard                  docs per shard
ranged, monotonic key     199  [100000, 0, 0, 0]                  [25500, 25000, 25000, 24500]
ranged, hashed(_id)       128  [29056, 23674, 24085, 23185]       [25382, 25036, 25327, 24255]
ranged, random key        131  [29367, 23494, 23137, 24002]       [25853, 23272, 25583, 25292]
country key: 8 distinct values, most frequent value IN = 55.0% of documents (55,040)
blocks.title: Shard key simulation (real output of the model, columns reformatted to fit the page)

blocks.text: Reading the result: with the monotonic key the stored data ends up balanced (about 25,000 documents on each shard, because the balancer migrated the old chunks away), yet shard 1 received all 100,000 inserts. The balancer repairs the storage skew but not the load skew, because every new document belongs to the newest chunk. The hashed and random keys spread the inserts within 18 percent of the ideal 25,000 per shard (the first shard is somewhat higher because chunks on it are split before they migrate). The last two lines show the frequency problem: an eight-valued key has 55 percent of its documents under one value, so the chunk of that value cannot be divided.

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

#### Creating a sharded collection

The commands below show the common sequence for the orders collection with a hashed customer key. They are typical output; no MongoDB cluster is available on the build machine.

**mongosh session against a mongos (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.code:
[direct: mongos] test> sh.shardCollection('shop.orders', { customerId: 'hashed' })
{
  collectionsharded: 'shop.orders',
  ok: 1,
  '$clusterTime': { clusterTime: Timestamp({ t: 1760257500, i: 8 }) }
}
[direct: mongos] test> db.getSiblingDB('shop').orders.getShardDistribution()
Shard shardA at shardA/a1:27018,a2:27018,a3:27018
  data : 3.91GiB docs : 4012331 chunks : 2
  estimated data per chunk : 1.95GiB estimated docs per chunk : 2006165
Shard shardB at shardB/b1:27018,b2:27018,b3:27018
  data : 3.88GiB docs : 3991020 chunks : 2
  estimated data per chunk : 1.94GiB estimated docs per chunk : 1995510
Totals
  data : 7.79GiB docs : 8003351 chunks : 4
  Shard shardA contains 50.13% data, 50.13% docs in cluster, avg obj size on shard : 1KiB
  Shard shardB contains 49.87% data, 49.87% docs in cluster, avg obj size on shard : 1KiB

blocks.text:
A hashed key on an empty collection creates initial chunks automatically (the option `numInitialChunks` controls how many), so the load is spread from the first insert; a ranged key starts with a single chunk on one shard and needs time to split and migrate.

#### Explaining a targeted and a scatter-gather query

**explain output reduced to the routing information (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.code:
[direct: mongos] shop> db.orders.find({ customerId: 5434 }).explain().queryPlanner.winningPlan
{ stage: 'SINGLE_SHARD',
  shards: [ { shardName: 'shardB', winningPlan: { stage: 'FETCH',
      inputStage: { stage: 'IXSCAN', indexName: 'customerId_hashed' } } } ] }
[direct: mongos] shop> db.orders.find({ status: 'NEW' }).explain().queryPlanner.winningPlan
{ stage: 'SHARD_MERGE',
  shards: [ { shardName: 'shardA', winningPlan: { stage: 'COLLSCAN' } },
            { shardName: 'shardB', winningPlan: { stage: 'COLLSCAN' } } ] }

blocks.text:
`SINGLE_SHARD` means one shard was contacted. `SHARD_MERGE` means several shards ran the query and mongos merged the results. The second query also shows a `COLLSCAN` on every shard: scatter-gather multiplies a missing index by the number of shards.

#### Zone commands

blocks.code:
sh.shardCollection('shop.customers', { region: 1, customerId: 1 })
sh.addShardToZone('shardA', 'IN')
sh.addShardToZone('shardB', 'EU')
sh.updateZoneKeyRange('shop.customers', { region: 'IN', customerId: MinKey },
                      { region: 'IN', customerId: MaxKey }, 'IN')
sh.updateZoneKeyRange('shop.customers', { region: 'EU', customerId: MinKey },
                      { region: 'EU', customerId: MaxKey }, 'EU')

blocks.text:
### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: shard key causing a hot shard

**Scenario.** An event collection is sharded on `{ createdAt: 1 }` ("because queries are by date"). The cluster has four shards and the dashboards show a balanced disk usage.

**Symptoms.** The primary of one shard runs at 95 percent CPU and has a growing write queue; the other three are almost idle. Insert latency rises with load although the cluster has spare capacity. `sh.status()` reports balanced chunk counts.

**Diagnosis.** In order:

1. Compare per-shard operation counters: `db.serverStatus().opcounters` on each shard primary (or the monitoring graphs per shard). One shard shows nearly all inserts.
2. Identify the chunk that receives the inserts: `db.getSiblingDB('config').chunks.find({ ns: 'shop.events'` `}).sort({ min: -1 }).limit(1)` shows the chunk with the highest key range and its shard.
3. Check the shard key analysis for monotonicity: `db.events.analyzeShardKey({ createdAt: 1 })` (MongoDB 7.0 and later) reports a monotonic change in the key; for earlier versions the inference follows from the key being a timestamp.

**Root cause.** A monotonically increasing ranged key sends every insert to the chunk with the maximum key, which lives on one shard. The balancer moves older chunks to other shards, so storage is balanced but the write load is not. The experiment in the worked example reproduces the effect: 100,000 inserts on one shard and none on the others.

**Fix.** Immediate: add capacity to the hot shard's primary (vertical scaling) and reduce write amplification (fewer indexes, batching). Permanent: reshard to a key with a non-monotonic component, for example `{ deviceId: 1,` `createdAt: 1 }` (writes spread by device, time queries per device targeted) or `{ createdAt: 'hashed' }` when range queries on time are rare. Run `reshardCollection` outside the peak and verify spare disk space (a full copy of the collection).

**Prevention.** Evaluate candidate keys with `analyzeShardKey` and a load test before sharding; reject timestamps, `ObjectId` and sequences as the first field of a ranged key; monitor operation counters per shard.

#### Incident: jumbo chunks

**Scenario.** Orders are sharded by `{ country: 1 }`. The business operates mostly in one country.

**Symptoms.** One shard holds 55 percent of the data and its disk fills first. `sh.status()` marks chunks as `jumbo: true`. Migrations of those chunks fail or are skipped, and the balancer logs that the chunk "exceeds the maximum size and cannot be split". **Diagnosis.**

1. `db.getSiblingDB('config').chunks.find({ ns: 'shop.orders', jumbo: true })` lists the flagged chunks and their key ranges. In the typical case min and max of the chunk have the same `country` value.
2. `db.orders.aggregate([{ $group: { _id: '$country', n: { $sum: 1 } } }, { $sort: { n: -1 } }])` shows the frequency distribution: here 55 percent of the documents carry `IN`.
3. `db.orders.stats().avgObjSize` multiplied by the document count of the range gives the chunk size and confirms that it exceeds the range size.

**Root cause.** A chunk is bounded by key values; documents with the same key value cannot be separated. The key has too few distinct values and a dominant one.

**Fix.** Immediate: for a temporary relief, `sh.splitAt` cannot split a single value, so free space by archiving old data or increasing the shard's disk; `moveRange` with `forceJumbo` can migrate an oversized range explicitly when the destination has room. Permanent: refine the key by appending a high-cardinality field, `db.adminCommand({` `refineCollectionShardKey: 'shop.orders', key: { country: 1, customerId: 1 } })` (the index on the new key must exist first), after which the dominant value can be split by `customerId`; or reshard.

**Prevention.** Check the frequency distribution of candidate keys against production data; use compound keys that end with a high-cardinality field; alert when any chunk is flagged jumbo.

#### Incident: scatter-gather queries after sharding

**Scenario.** A collection is sharded on `{ customerId: 'hashed' }`. A support page searches orders by `orderNumber`.

**Symptoms.** The query took 4 ms on a replica set and takes 60 ms on the cluster and consumes CPU on every shard. Explain shows `SHARD_MERGE`.

**Diagnosis.** `explain()` on mongos lists all shards; the filter lacks the shard key. `db.currentOp()` on each shard shows the same query running concurrently.

**Root cause.** The filter does not contain the shard key, so mongos cannot target a shard. The cost grows with the number of shards.

**Fix.** Immediate: add an index on `orderNumber` on every shard (each shard still runs the query, but as an index lookup). Permanent: include the customer id in the lookup (the page knows the customer), or create a lookup collection `orderIndex` keyed by `orderNumber` that stores the customer id, or choose a shard key that serves the dominant access path.

**Prevention.** Review the top queries for the presence of the shard key before sharding; track scatter-gather ratio in monitoring (`serverStatus().metrics.query.scatterGather` where available).

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **What is a shard key and why is it important?** The field(s) that decide which shard owns a document. It determines write distribution, query targeting and the ability to split chunks; a poor key causes hot shards, jumbo chunks or scatter-gather queries.
2. **Ranged versus hashed sharding?** Ranged keeps neighbouring values together (good range queries, risk of hot spots with monotonic keys). Hashed spreads values uniformly (good write distribution, range queries become scatter-gather).
3. **What are cardinality, frequency and monotonicity?** The number of distinct values, how evenly they occur, and whether new values only increase. Low cardinality, skewed frequency and monotonic growth each cause imbalance.
4. **What does mongos do?** It routes operations using the cached chunk map, merges results from several shards, and hides the cluster layout from the application.
5. **How does the balancer work?** It runs on the config server primary, compares data size per shard, and migrates ranges when the difference exceeds three range sizes, one migration per shard at a time.
6. **What is a jumbo chunk?** A chunk that exceeds the range size and cannot be split or moved, usually because all documents share one key value. Remedy: refine the shard key or reshard.
7. **Can the shard key be changed?** Yes: refine it by adding fields (4.4), or reshard to a different key online (5.0). Field values can be updated (4.2) except `_id`.
8. **Why must unique indexes include the shard key?** Each shard enforces uniqueness only locally; including the shard key guarantees that equal values land on the same shard.
9. **What does zone sharding provide?** Placement of key ranges on chosen shards, for data residency or hardware tiers.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The shard key is the most consequential design decision of a sharded cluster.

- Good keys have high cardinality, even frequency, non-monotonic writes and appear in the common filters.
- Chunks default to 128 MB; the balancer evens out stored data, not insert load.
- Queries with the shard key are targeted; others are broadcast to all shards.
- Zones pin key ranges to shards; resharding and key refinement correct a wrong choice at a cost in time and disk space.

Operating MongoDB means understanding where data lives, what must fit in memory, how a write reaches the disk, how to take a backup that restores, how to find the operation that is slow right now, and how to close the default security gaps. This chapter explains the WiredTiger storage engine, sizing by working set, backup methods, monitoring tools and the security controls that matter, and it ends with a decision path for a slow cluster. Atlas, the managed service, is mentioned only where it changes a recommendation; the facts below apply to self-managed deployments.

### Concept and mechanism

#### WiredTiger

WiredTiger has been the default storage engine since MongoDB 3.2. It organises each collection and each index as a B-tree file (`collection-*.wt`, `index-*.wt`) and keeps two representations of the data: in-memory pages in its own cache, and compressed blocks on disk.

- **Cache.** The default size is the larger of 50 percent of (RAM minus 1 GB) and 256 MB. The cache holds uncompressed pages for collections and indexes, plus dirty pages waiting to be written. The operating system file cache holds the compressed blocks as a second level. Pages are evicted when the cache fills; when dirty data exceeds thresholds, application threads help with eviction and latency rises.
- **Journal.** Every change is first recorded in a write-ahead journal. The journal is flushed to disk about every 100 ms, and immediately for writes with `j: true` or `w: "majority"` (which implies the journal on a majority). After a crash, mongod replays the journal from the last checkpoint.
- **Checkpoints.** About every 60 seconds WiredTiger writes a consistent snapshot of all data to the data files. The previous checkpoint stays valid until the new one is complete, so the data files are always consistent as of some checkpoint.
- **Compression.** Collections use snappy block compression by default (zstd and zlib are options; time series collections default to zstd). Indexes use prefix compression, which stores shared key prefixes once.
- **Concurrency.** Locking is at document level. Operations that touch different documents of the same collection proceed in parallel; conflicting writes to one document are retried internally. Since MongoDB 7.0 the number of concurrent storage transactions (read and write tickets) is adjusted dynamically up to a maximum of 128 each.

blocks.text:
A crash with the default settings can lose at most the last journal interval (about 100 ms) of writes acknowledged with `w: 1` and no `j`. For `w: "majority"` the loss window does not exist on a majority of members. This matters only for a standalone or for `w: 1`; in a replica set the surviving members hold the data.

#### Working set and memory

The working set is the data and indexes that the workload touches regularly. When it fits in the WiredTiger cache plus the operating system cache, reads are served from memory; when it does not, every cache miss costs a disk read of a page, one or two orders of magnitude slower. Indexes matter most: an index that does not fit forces page reads at every level of every lookup. A practical sizing rule is that all indexes and the hot part of the data fit in memory. The size of the indexes is reported by `db.collection.stats().indexSizes`, and the cache occupancy by `serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache`.

The access pattern determines how much memory is enough. A model run on the build machine shows the effect: an LRU cache in front of 200,000 pages (a page per document), with accesses drawn from a skewed (Zipf) distribution that resembles real data, versus a uniform distribution that touches everything equally. The average latency assumes 0.1 ms for a memory hit and 5 ms for a disk read, which are illustrative values.

blocks.text:
The conclusion for sizing is that the shape of the access pattern matters more than the dataset size: a skewed workload tolerates a cache much smaller than the data, whereas a workload that scans or samples uniformly (analytics over the whole collection, random lookups over all customers) needs the data in memory or tolerates disk latency.

#### Backup and restore

rows: logical; with --oplog a consistent dump of a replica set
slow to dump and to restore (rebuilds indexes); suited to small data sets and migrations
consistent when journal and data are on the same volume
fast; needs a snapshot-capable volume; sharded clusters need coordinated snapshots
any time inside the archived oplog
the basis of point-in-time recovery; offered by managed services and backup tools
a safety net, not a backup

blocks.text: For a sharded cluster a consistent backup needs all shards and the config servers captured at the same logical moment, with the balancer stopped (`sh.stopBalancer()`), or a tool that coordinates this. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the age of the newest recoverable data; the recovery time objective (RTO) is the time to restore. A restore must be rehearsed regularly: a backup that was never restored is an assumption. A typical logical backup and restore:

blocks.code:
$ mongodump --uri "mongodb://db1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0" --oplog --gzip --out /backup/2026-10-12
2026-10-12T02:00:01.114+0000    writing shop.orders to /backup/2026-10-12/shop/orders.bson.gz
2026-10-12T02:00:41.870+0000    done dumping shop.orders (8003351 documents)
2026-10-12T02:00:42.002+0000    writing captured oplog to
$ mongorestore --uri "mongodb://newdb1:27017" --oplogReplay --gzip /backup/2026-10-12
blocks.title: Logical backup with the oplog and restore (typical output, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
#### Monitoring and diagnosis tools

Four sources answer most operational questions.

- `db.serverStatus()` returns counters and gauges: `opcounters` (operations per second when sampled twice), `connections` (current and available), `wiredTiger.cache` (bytes in cache, dirty bytes, maximum), `globalLock`, `queues.execution` (queued read and write tickets), `repl` and `metrics`. Monitoring systems sample it and plot the deltas.
- `db.currentOp()` lists running operations with their duration (`secs_running`), the namespace, the query and whether they are waiting for a lock (`waitingForLock`). `db.killOp(opid)` stops one.
- The database profiler records slow operations in the capped collection `system.profile` of each database. `db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 100 })` records operations slower than 100 ms (the default threshold); level 2 records everything and is for short diagnostic windows only.
- `explain('executionStats')` shows how one query ran; the ratio `totalDocsExamined` to `nReturned` is the first indicator of a missing or poor index (see the chapter on indexes and explain).

**Finding slow and blocked operations (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.code:
shop> db.currentOp({ active: true, secs_running: { $gt: 5 } }).inprog.map(o =>
...   ({ opid: o.opid, ns: o.ns, secs: o.secs_running, waiting: o.waitingForLock, op: o.op }))
[ { opid: 982341, ns: 'shop.orders', secs: 41, waiting: false, op: 'query' } ]
shop> db.getSiblingDB('shop').system.profile.find({ millis: { $gt: 100 } })
...   .sort({ ts: -1 }).limit(1)
[ { op: 'query', ns: 'shop.orders', command: { find: 'orders', filter: { status: 'NEW' } },
    keysExamined: 0, docsExamined: 4012331, nreturned: 118, planSummary: 'COLLSCAN',
    millis: 2874, ts: ISODate('2026-10-12T08:41:00.221Z') } ]
shop> db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache['tracked dirty bytes in the cache']
412763904

blocks.text: The profile entry shows the typical signature of a missing index: `docsExamined` of 4,012,331 for 118 documents returned, with plan `COLLSCAN`.

#### Security

MongoDB started with authentication disabled by default in older versions, which produced a long list of exposed databases. The controls below are the baseline for any deployment.

blocks.alt: Network bind_ip, firewall, private subnets, no public port 27017 | Transport TLS between clients, mongos and members (net.tls.mode requireTLS) | Authentication SCRAM-SHA-256, x.509, LDAP / OIDC; keyfile or x.509 for members | Authorization role-based access control: least-privilege custom roles | Input handling bind values as typed parameters; reject operator objects | Auditing authentication, DDL and role changes logged | Encryption at rest encrypted storage volume or enterprise encrypted storage engine

blocks.text:
- **Authentication and authorization.** `security.authorization: enabled` turns on access control; clients authenticate with SCRAM-SHA-256 (default), x.509 certificates or an external provider. Members of a replica set authenticate to one another with a keyfile or x.509 certificates. Roles grant privileges on resources: `read`, `readWrite`, `dbAdmin`, `clusterMonitor`, and custom roles. The application user receives `readWrite` on its own database only.
- **Transport encryption.** `net.tls.mode: requireTLS` encrypts client and internal traffic.
- **Network.** `net.bindIp` restricts listening addresses; the port is never reachable from the internet; a firewall or private subnet restricts clients to the application hosts.
- **Encryption at rest.** An encrypted volume protects against lost disks; MongoDB Enterprise offers an encrypted storage engine and client-side field-level encryption for selected fields.
- **Auditing.** Authentication events, DDL and role changes are logged (Enterprise audit log, or Atlas).

**Creating a least-privilege application user (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

admin> use shop
shop> db.createUser({ user: 'orders_app', pwd: passwordPrompt(),
...   roles: [{ role: 'readWrite', db: 'shop' }] })

blocks.text:
#### Operator injection

MongoDB queries are documents, so a value that the application takes from a request can itself be an operator document. A login endpoint that passes the parsed JSON body straight into a filter accepts `{ "username": "admin",` `"password": { "$ne": null } }`: the password condition becomes "not equal to null" and matches every user. This is the NoSQL counterpart of SQL injection; it needs no string concatenation at all.

blocks.title: VulnerableLogin.java (fragment, not run: Spring Data MongoDB not available)

blocks.text:
The fix has three parts: bind request bodies to typed objects (a `String` field cannot hold an operator document), never build queries from raw maps or from JSON strings, and compare hashed passwords in application code. Server-side JavaScript (`$where`, `mapReduce` functions) can be disabled with `security.javascriptEnabled: false` when no application uses it.

### Worked example

A cluster has a WiredTiger cache of 15 GB (a 32 GB host: 0.5 times (32 minus 1) is 15.5 GB, rounded down). The orders collection has 90 GB of data and 14 GB of indexes. The hot part of the data is the last 30 days, about 8 GB. The question is whether this host is adequately sized.

1. Indexes alone (14 GB) nearly fill the cache of 15 GB. Together with the hot data (8 GB) the working set is 22 GB, larger than the cache.
2. The operating system cache holds compressed blocks: with snappy compression at roughly 2:1 for typical JSON-like documents, 8 GB of hot data occupies about 4 GB compressed. The OS cache has about 32 minus 15 minus 3 (process and connections) = 14 GB available, so the compressed hot data fits there, but every access through it needs a decompression and a copy into the WiredTiger cache.
3. Expect a cache hit ratio well below the skewed curve in the experiment: the cache is full of index pages and constant eviction takes place. `serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache['pages read into cache']` grows steadily and the dirty fraction is high.
4. Options in order of cost: drop unused indexes (`db.orders.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }])` shows `accesses.ops` per index; unused indexes consume cache for nothing), reduce index size with partial indexes, add RAM (64 GB host gives a 31.5 GB cache), or shard so each shard holds a smaller working set.

The first step costs nothing and is applied first; the decision to add RAM follows the measurement after cleaning the indexes.

### Hands-on

#### A first look at a deployment

**Health snapshot of a mongod (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

The numbers read as follows: the cache is at 99 percent of its maximum, which is normal for a busy server (a full cache is not a problem by itself; high eviction and read rates are); the dirty fraction is 2.6 percent, below the eviction thresholds; tickets are plentiful, so there is no concurrency bottleneck; replication lag is zero. A low `available` ticket count alone does not indicate overload; a growing queue does.

#### Index usage report

**Finding indexes that waste cache (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.code:
shop> db.orders.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} },
...   { $project: { name: 1, ops: '$accesses.ops', since: '$accesses.since' } }])
[ { name: '_id_', ops: Long('881204551'), since: ISODate('2026-09-01T00:00:00.000Z') },
  { name: 'customerId_1_createdAt_-1', ops: Long('12044871'),
    since: ISODate('2026-09-01T00:00:00.000Z') },
  { name: 'status_1', ops: Long('0'), since: ISODate('2026-09-01T00:00:00.000Z') } ]

blocks.text:
The index `status_1` was never used since the statistics began; it costs write time and cache space and is a candidate for removal (hide it first with `db.orders.hideIndex('status_1')` to confirm that nothing slows down, then drop it).

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: working set exceeding RAM

**Scenario.** A product search service runs for months with latency of 5 ms. Over three weeks the catalogue doubles and a new index is added for a filter.

**Symptoms.** p95 latency rises to 200 ms. CPU is low, disk read IOPS are at the volume limit. No query plan changed.

**Diagnosis.**

1. `db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache` compared over 60 seconds: `pages read into cache` is rising rapidly and `bytes currently in the cache` sits at the maximum.
2. `db.products.stats().indexSizes` summed against the cache size: the indexes now exceed the cache.
3. OS metrics: `iostat -x` shows high read utilisation on the data volume; the page cache hit rate dropped.
4. `$indexStats` shows an index with no use.

**Root cause.** The working set (indexes plus hot data) no longer fits in memory, so lookups that used to hit the cache now read from disk. The access pattern is close to uniform because the new filter makes users page through the whole catalogue, which corresponds to the "uniform" column of the model: hit ratio equals the cache fraction.

**Fix.** Immediate: hide and drop the unused index; scale the host to more memory. Permanent: reduce index size (partial indexes, remove redundant prefixes: `{a:1}` is redundant to `{a:1,b:1}`), archive cold documents, and, when a single host cannot hold the working set, shard by a key that keeps related data together.

**Prevention.** Alert on cache read rates and index size relative to cache; review index usage monthly; capacity-plan memory from index size growth.

#### Incident: operator injection in a login endpoint

**Scenario.** A Spring Boot endpoint authenticates users through MongoDB and passes a request map to the query.

**Symptoms.** The security scan reports that sending `{"username":"admin","password":{"$ne":null}}` returns a valid session; access logs show unusual JSON bodies containing `$`-prefixed keys.

**Diagnosis.** Reproduce with `curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d` `'{"username":"admin","password":{"$ne":null}}' https://host/login`; inspect the controller for `Map<String,` `Object>` or `BasicQuery` constructed from the body; confirm with the profiler that the logged filter contains the operator.

**Root cause.** Untyped input is interpreted as a query document, so the attacker chooses the operators.

**Fix.** Immediate: block requests with keys starting with `$` at the gateway and rotate sessions. Permanent: typed DTOs, validation, server-side password hashing and comparison (see the listing above), and the least-privilege database user so that the application account cannot read other databases.

**Prevention.** Static analysis rule against `BasicQuery(new Document(map))` and `Document.parse(userInput)`; security tests that send operator payloads.

#### Incident: restore that did not work

**Scenario.** A collection is dropped by mistake. The team restores last night's `mongodump`.

**Symptoms.** The restore takes 9 hours and the application is down; afterwards indexes are missing or the restore reports duplicate key errors because the target was not empty.

**Diagnosis.** `mongorestore` output and the restore log; `db.orders.getIndexes()` after the restore; timing of the dump (it was taken without `--oplog` on a busy primary, so it is not a consistent point in time across collections).

**Root cause.** A logical backup restores documents and then rebuilds every index, which is slow for large data; the dump was not consistent; and the procedure was never rehearsed.

**Fix.** Immediate: restore into a separate database to recover the dropped collection only (`--nsInclude shop.orders` `--nsFrom ... --nsTo ...`), then copy back. Permanent: take volume snapshots with oplog archiving for point-in-time recovery, use `--oplog` for dumps, and schedule restore drills that record the elapsed time as the real RTO.

**Prevention.** Keep a delayed secondary for logical errors, restrict `drop` privileges, and test the restore monthly.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **What is the WiredTiger cache and how large is it by default?** The engine's cache of uncompressed pages; default is the larger of 50 percent of (RAM minus 1 GB) or 256 MB. The OS cache holds the compressed file blocks.
2. **How does MongoDB survive a crash?** Changes are written to the journal before they are acknowledged with `j:` `true` or `w: "majority"`; after a crash, the data is restored from the last checkpoint (taken every 60 seconds) and the journal is replayed.
3. **What is the working set?** The data and indexes touched by the regular workload. Performance degrades sharply when it exceeds available memory.
4. **How do you find a slow query?** The profiler (`system.profile`), the slow query log, `db.currentOp()` for running operations, and `explain('executionStats')` to compare `docsExamined` with `nReturned`.
5. **mongodump or snapshots?** `mongodump` is logical and portable but slow to restore; snapshots are fast and, combined with oplog archiving, give point-in-time recovery. Both need rehearsed restores.
6. **What is NoSQL injection and how is it prevented?** Operator objects in user input (`$ne`, `$gt`, `$where`) change the query semantics. Prevent with typed DTOs, never passing raw maps into queries, validating input, and disabling server-side JavaScript.
7. **What are the minimum security settings?** Authentication enabled with least-privilege roles, TLS, restricted `bindIp` and network access, encrypted storage, and auditing.
8. **Why can a full WiredTiger cache be normal?** The cache is meant to be used; the signals of trouble are a high rate of pages read into cache, heavy eviction and a high dirty percentage, not the fill level.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
WiredTiger keeps uncompressed pages in a cache, protects changes with a journal and writes checkpoints every 60 seconds.

- Size memory for indexes plus the hot data; skewed access tolerates less memory than uniform access.
- Backups are logical (`mongodump`) or snapshot based; point-in-time recovery needs oplog archiving; rehearse restores.
- `serverStatus`, `currentOp`, the profiler and `explain` cover most diagnosis; start with examined-to-returned ratio.
- Enable authentication, TLS and least privilege, and never pass untyped request data into a query.

Spring Data MongoDB maps Java objects to BSON documents and offers two programming models over the MongoDB Java driver: repositories, which derive queries from method names, and `MongoTemplate`, which exposes the full query, update and aggregation API. A Spring Boot application obtains a configured `MongoClient`, a `MongoTemplate` and repository support from the `spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb` dependency and a connection URI. The abstraction is thin: every repository method becomes a driver call, and every design decision from the previous chapters (embedding, write concern, indexes, transactions) remains the responsibility of the developer. This chapter shows a complete service, explains where the abstraction hides cost (references, lazy loading, missing indexes, transactions), and lists the configuration that production needs. No Spring or MongoDB artifacts are available on the build machine, so all code in this chapter is unverified against a running system: it was written against the documented API of Spring Boot 3.x with Spring Data MongoDB 4.x (the API shown is also valid in the 5.x line that follows it) and checked only for Java syntax by the book's linter. Class names and annotations should be checked against the version in use.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Layers of the stack

A call such as `orderRepository.findByStatus(NEW)` passes through the repository proxy (query derivation), `MongoTemplate` (execution), the `MappingMongoConverter` (translation between Java objects and `Document`), and the driver (connection pool, server selection, retries), before reaching mongod or mongos. The converter writes the field `_class` with the fully qualified class name into each document so that polymorphic reads can instantiate the right type; this is a frequent cause of trouble after package renames, because stored documents still carry the old name.

blocks.text: #### Mapping annotations

rows: Marks an aggregate root and names the collection (default: decapitalised class name)
The `_id` field; a `String` or `ObjectId` property is generated by the driver on save
Stored field name; shorter names save space in every document
Single-field index (created only when auto index creation is enabled)
Optimistic locking: the version is checked and incremented on every save
Filled by auditing when `@EnableMongoAuditing` is present
Stores a reference to a document in another collection and loads it (eagerly by default, lazily with `lazy = true`)
Reference with a configurable lookup (3.3 and later); stores a plain id, loads through a query
blocks.caption: Core mapping annotations.

blocks.text:
#### Repositories, templates and aggregation

`MongoRepository<T, ID>` provides `save`, `findById`, `findAll(Pageable)`, `deleteById` and `count`, plus derived queries: the method name `findByCustomerIdAndStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc` is parsed into a filter and a sort. `@Query` takes a JSON filter with positional parameters (`?0`), and `@Aggregation` accepts pipeline stages as JSON. `MongoTemplate` offers the programmatic API: `Query` with `Criteria`, `Update` for partial updates (`$set`, `$inc`, `$push`), `findAndModify` for atomic read-modify-write, and `aggregate` with a typed `Aggregation` pipeline. Partial updates through `Update` are preferable to `save(entity)` for hot fields, because `save` replaces the whole document and can overwrite concurrent changes to other fields.

#### Transactions in Spring

`@Transactional` on a service method uses the registered `PlatformTransactionManager`. For MongoDB the manager is `MongoTransactionManager`, and it must be declared as a bean: Spring Boot does not register one automatically, so without it `@Transactional` has no effect on MongoDB operations (the methods simply run without a transaction). The manager starts a driver session and a transaction at method entry, binds the session to the thread, and commits at normal return or aborts on a runtime exception (checked exceptions do not trigger rollback unless `rollbackFor` says so, as for any Spring transaction). Transactions require a replica set or sharded cluster; on a standalone mongod, the first operation fails with "Transaction numbers are only allowed on a replica set member or mongos". The same rules as for relational transactions apply: the proxy is bypassed by self-invocation, so a `@Transactional` method called from another method of the same class does not start a transaction.

blocks.text:
### Worked example

The example is the order service of the e-commerce domain used in this book. It consists of the build file entries, the entity, the repository, a service with a transaction, a controller and the configuration. The orders embed their items and a snapshot of the customer's name, following the design rules of the schema design chapter; stock is a separate collection because it is updated independently.

#### Dependencies and configuration
