spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation=false
blocks.title: application.properties (unverified)

blocks.text:
The URI carries the write concern, the pool bounds and the timeouts; `auto-index-creation` is false by default and stays false in production, where indexes are created by a controlled migration so that an application start never triggers a large index build. The driver pool defaults to a maximum of 100 connections per server.

#### Entity

blocks.title: Order.java (unverified)

blocks.text:
What to notice: `BigDecimal` is stored as a string by default in Spring Data MongoDB unless a Decimal128 representation is configured through the converter customisation (`MongoCustomConversions`; recent versions offer a BigDecimal representation option, to be confirmed for the version in use), so arithmetic and range queries on `total` need that configuration; the field `version` makes `save` fail with `OptimisticLockingFailureException` when two writers update the same order concurrently; the enum is stored by name.

#### Repository

blocks.title: OrderRepository.java (unverified)

blocks.text:
The first method derives the filter `{ customerId: ?, }` and the sort `{ createdAt: -1 }` and uses the compound index `customer_created`. Paging with `Pageable` translates into `skip` and `limit`; for deep pages the offset cost described in the indexes chapter applies, so a range filter on `createdAt` or `_id` is preferable for long lists. The `@Aggregation` method is the repository form of the revenue pipeline from the aggregation chapter. (Note: in `topCustomers`, the `$sum` of a total stored as a string yields 0; see the `BigDecimal` remark above.)

#### Service with a transaction

blocks.title: OrderService.java (unverified)

blocks.text:
What to notice: the stock decrement uses a conditional update (`qty >= requested`) so that two concurrent orders cannot both take the last unit, even without a transaction, because the update of one document is atomic. The transaction adds the property that a failure in the third item restores the stock taken for the first two. `markPaid` is a single-document write and does not need `@Transactional`; the annotation is kept for the example and costs a session start. The state transition `NEW` to `PAID` is expressed as a filter, which makes it an atomic compare-and-set.

#### Controller, configuration, auditing

blocks.title: OrderController.java (unverified)
MongoConfig.java (unverified)

blocks.text:
The customizer sets the properties that cannot be expressed as readable URI options: majority write concern and a short wait for a pooled connection (`maxWaitTime`), so that pool exhaustion surfaces as an error after two seconds and not as a hung request thread.

blocks.text:
#### Testing

Repository and service tests need a real MongoDB because query semantics, indexes and transactions are server behaviour. Two options exist, both described here and not run on the build machine. The first uses Testcontainers: the class `MongoDBContainer` starts a single-node replica set (which is what transactions require), and in Spring Boot 3.1 and later the annotation `@ServiceConnection` wires the application to it. The second embeds a MongoDB binary through Flapdoodle, which is lighter but trails the server version. Unit tests of controllers mock the service and need no database.

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

#### The queries behind the repository

Enabling the logger `org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.MongoTemplate` at `DEBUG` prints each query that Spring Data sends. The log lines below are typical output (not run); they show the filters that the repository methods generate.

**Log output with MongoTemplate at DEBUG (typical output, not run)**

blocks.code:
find using query: { "customerId" : 5434 } for class: class Order in collection: orders
find using query: { "status" : "NEW", "items.sku" : "A-100" } in collection: orders
Executing aggregation: [{ "$match" : { "status" : { "$in" : ["PAID", "SHIPPED"] } } }, ..

blocks.text:
#### Creating the indexes outside the application

With `auto-index-creation=false` the indexes that the annotations describe must exist from another source. A migration script run by the deployment pipeline (a shell script, or a migration library such as Mongock) creates them. In a replica set, indexes build on every member; on a large collection the build runs in the background of the server but uses I/O and cache.

**Index migration (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.code:
shop> db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 }, { name: 'customer_created' })
customer_created
shop> db.orders.createIndex({ status: 1 }, { name: 'status_1' })
status_1
shop> db.orders.getIndexes().map(i => i.name)
[ '_id_', 'customer_created', 'status_1' ]

blocks.text:
#### Detecting N+1 from the server side

The server's profiler or a monitoring counter shows the pattern independent of the framework: many `find` commands on the referenced collection with `_id` filters within one request.

**Profiler view of an N+1 pattern (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.code:
shop> db.setProfilingLevel(2)
shop> db.system.profile.aggregate([
...   { $match: { op: 'query', ns: 'shop.customers' } },
...   { $group: { _id: { $dateTrunc: { date: '$ts', unit: 'second' } }, queries: { $sum: 1 } } },
...   { $sort: { _id: -1 } }, { $limit: 3 } ])
[ { _id: ISODate('2026-10-12T09:12:44.000Z'), queries: 5100 },
  { _id: ISODate('2026-10-12T09:12:43.000Z'), queries: 4980 },
  { _id: ISODate('2026-10-12T09:12:42.000Z'), queries: 5075 } ]

blocks.text:
About 5,000 point queries per second on `customers` while the endpoint receives 100 requests per second is the signature: 50 customer lookups per request.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: N+1 queries from @DBRef

**Scenario.** The order list endpoint returns 50 orders with the customer's name. The `Order` class holds `@DBRef Customer` `customer`. The endpoint was fast in development with 5 orders.

**Symptoms.** In production the endpoint takes 400 ms at p50; MongoDB CPU is high with a very high query rate on `customers`; the application log with MongoTemplate at DEBUG prints dozens of `find using query: { "_id" : ... }` lines per request.

**Diagnosis.** In order:

1. Count the queries of one request in the application log (DEBUG logger above): 51 for 50 orders.
2. Confirm from the server: the profiler query shown above, or `db.serverStatus().opcounters.query` sampled during one request.
3. Inspect the mapping: `@DBRef` without `lazy` loads the reference eagerly, one query per referenced document, and lazy loading only moves the same queries to the first access.

**Root cause.** A DBRef is resolved by the client, one lookup per reference; MongoDB performs no join on read. The N+1 pattern of Hibernate lazy loading appears here in a different place, with a network round trip per reference.

**Fix.** Immediate: replace the data that the list needs by a snapshot in the order (`customerId`, `customerName`), written at order creation (extended reference pattern); the list endpoint then runs one query. If the live customer data is required, resolve it with one batched query: `customerRepository.findAllById(ids)` and map in memory, or one aggregation with `$lookup`. Permanent: use `@DocumentReference` or plain ids for references, embed the fields that are read with the parent, and keep the number of queries per request as a metric.

**Prevention.** A request-level assertion in integration tests on the number of commands (using a `CommandListener` registered with the driver); code review rule against `@DBRef` on read-heavy paths.

#### Incident: @Transactional has no effect on MongoDB

**Scenario.** A service method debits stock and saves an order inside `@Transactional`. A test forces an exception after the stock update and expects the stock to be restored.

**Symptoms.** The stock stays decremented after the exception. Alternatively, on a development laptop with a standalone mongod, every call fails with `Transaction numbers are only allowed on a replica set member or` `mongos`.

**Diagnosis.**

1. Check that a `MongoTransactionManager` bean exists: `applicationContext.getBeansOfType(PlatformTransactionManager.class)`. Spring Boot does not create one for MongoDB.
2. Check how the method is called: from another method of the same class (self-invocation bypasses the proxy), or the method is `private` or `final`, or it throws a checked exception (no rollback by default).
3. Check the server topology: `db.hello()` returns no `setName` field on a standalone mongod; transactions need a replica set.

**Root cause.** Without a `MongoTransactionManager`, the annotation is processed against no Mongo-aware manager (or another manager, for example a JPA one, that is irrelevant to MongoDB), so the writes run outside any transaction and each commits independently. The standalone error is the server refusing transaction numbers.

**Fix.** Declare the transaction manager bean (see the configuration class), run development databases as single-node replica sets (`mongod --replSet rs0` followed by `rs.initiate()`), call transactional methods through the Spring proxy (from another bean), and add `rollbackFor` for checked exceptions.

**Prevention.** An integration test per transactional use case that forces a failure and asserts the rollback, against the same MongoDB topology class as production (Testcontainers `MongoDBContainer`).

#### Incident: missing indexes in production because annotations were trusted

**Scenario.** The entity carries `@Indexed` and `@CompoundIndex`; the team assumes the indexes exist. In production `spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation` is false (the default).

**Symptoms.** A list endpoint that was fast on developers' machines (where the property was true) takes seconds in production; the profiler shows `COLLSCAN` with `docsExamined` in the millions.

**Diagnosis.** `db.orders.getIndexes()` in production lists only `_id_`; the profiler entries show `planSummary:` `'COLLSCAN'`; `explain('executionStats')` of the repository's query confirms it.

**Root cause.** The annotations declare intent; indexes are created only when automatic creation is enabled, which has been off by default since Spring Data MongoDB 3.0.

**Fix.** Create the indexes with the migration script shown in the hands-on section, in a quiet period for a large collection. Permanent: version index definitions with the code (migration tool), and verify in the deployment pipeline that every annotated index exists.

**Prevention.** A startup check or integration test that compares `getIndexes()` with the annotated indexes; do not enable auto creation in production, because an application start would trigger index builds.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **How do** `MongoRepository` **and** `MongoTemplate` **differ?** The repository derives queries from method names and is the default for simple access; `MongoTemplate` provides the full API (partial updates, `findAndModify`, aggregation, bulk operations) when derived queries are insufficient.
2. **How are transactions enabled with Spring Data MongoDB?** Register a `MongoTransactionManager` bean and annotate service methods with `@Transactional`; the deployment must be a replica set or sharded cluster.
3. **What is the N+1 problem with** `@DBRef`**?** Each reference is resolved by a separate client query, so loading N parents costs N+1 round trips. Embed a snapshot, batch the lookups with `findAllById`, or use `$lookup`.
4. **Why is** `save` **risky for hot documents?** It writes the entire document, so a concurrent change to another field can be lost; partial updates with `Update` (`$set`, `$inc`) or `@Version` avoid this.
5. **What does** `@Version` **do?** It adds optimistic locking: the update filter includes the expected version and a mismatch raises `OptimisticLockingFailureException`.
6. **How do you configure the connection pool?** Through URI options (`maxPoolSize`, `minPoolSize`, `maxIdleTimeMS`) or a `MongoClientSettingsBuilderCustomizer`; the wait time for a connection should be bounded.
7. **How do you test code that uses MongoDB?** Against a real server: Testcontainers with `MongoDBContainer` (a single-node replica set), or an embedded binary; mocking the repository tests only the service logic.
8. **Why is** `_class` **stored in documents and when does it hurt?** It enables polymorphic mapping; after a class is renamed or moved, old documents fail to map unless a `@TypeAlias` or a migration handles them.
9. **How does the application set the write concern and read preference?** In the URI (`w=majority`, `readPreference=...`) or on the client settings; `MongoTemplate` can override per template instance.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Spring Data MongoDB is a thin mapping layer: modelling, indexes, write concern and transactions remain explicit decisions.

- Declare a `MongoTransactionManager` and run on a replica set for `@Transactional` to take effect.
- Prefer embedded snapshots or batched lookups to `@DBRef`, which causes N+1 queries.
- Use partial updates and `@Version` instead of whole-document `save` on contended documents.
- Create indexes through migrations; do not rely on annotations or on automatic creation in production.
- Test against a real MongoDB replica set.

sections.title: Relational versus Non-Relational: A Head-to-Head Comparison

blocks.text:
### Comparison

The choice between a relational database and a document database is a choice of data model, consistency boundary and operating model, and it is often made on reputation. This chapter replaces reputation with measurement and rules. It models one domain, the e-commerce orders used throughout the book, in both ways, compares the two on queries, transactions, scale and operations, runs a benchmark on PostgreSQL 16 that includes the middle path (a JSONB column in a relational table), and gives decision rules, a migration procedure and hybrid architectures. PostgreSQL results are real (measured on the build machine, 2 CPUs, 8 GB shared with other jobs, `shared_buffers` 64 MB, so absolute timings are typical and only the ratios are meaningful). MongoDB statements are taken from the documentation and are not measured.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The same domain, two models

The domain consists of customers, products and orders with several items per order. The relational model normalises it into four tables and joins them at read time. The document model stores an order as one document that embeds its items and a copy of the data that is displayed with the order (customer name and city, product name and category), because an order must show what was true when it was placed.

blocks.title: Relational schema (PostgreSQL)

blocks.text: **Document model (mongosh)**

The document above has the shape of the real document that the benchmark generated in PostgreSQL, so the two models contain identical information. The benchmark data set has 50,000 customers, 2,000 products, 500,000 orders and 1,250,000 order items (between one and four items per order).

#### Comparison by dimension

rows: Normalised tables, foreign keys, one fact in one place
Aggregates with embedded data and copies; references where needed
Declared and enforced by the server (types, NOT NULL, CHECK, FK)
Flexible; optional `$jsonSchema` validation; enforced mainly by the application
Joins across tables; cost grows with joins
One document read; cost grows with document size
Strong: any join, any aggregate, mature optimiser
Aggregation pipeline and `$lookup`; weaker for many-way joins
Multi-statement ACID transactions are the normal tool
Single-document atomicity; multi-document transactions are supported but bounded
Update every copy, or accept stale copies
Serializable or read committed per transaction; immediate consistency on the primary
Majority write concern by default since 5.0; reads from secondaries are eventually consistent
Not built in (replicas scale reads; sharding by extension or partitioning)
Built in: sharding with balancer and zones
Streaming replication with external orchestration (Patroni, managed services)
B-tree, hash, GIN, GiST, BRIN, partial, expression
B-tree (single, compound, multikey), text, geospatial, TTL, wildcard
Missing index, lock contention, long transactions, bloat
Unbounded arrays, hot shard key, working set above RAM, schema drift
JDBC, Spring Data JPA (entities, lazy loading, N+1)
MongoDB driver, Spring Data MongoDB (embedded documents, @DBRef N+1)
blocks.caption: Relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL) versus document (MongoDB).

blocks.text:
#### JSONB, the middle path

PostgreSQL stores JSON in the binary type `jsonb` with operators for containment (`@>`), key existence (`?`), path extraction (`->`, `->>`, `#>>`), the SQL/JSON path language (`@?`, `jsonb_path_query`), and index support: GIN indexes (`jsonb_ops` or the smaller `jsonb_path_ops`) for containment and existence queries, and B-tree expression indexes for scalar paths. A `jsonb` column inside a relational table provides flexible attributes while keeping transactions, constraints, joins and the existing operational tooling. MySQL 8 offers a `JSON` type with functional indexes on generated columns and multi-valued indexes over arrays, with a narrower feature set. The trade-offs are structural: a `jsonb` value is stored and updated as a whole, so changing one field rewrites the entire value (and its TOAST data when large); statistics are not collected inside the value, so the planner estimates containment predicates with fixed defaults; and the shape is not enforced unless a `CHECK` constraint says so.

### Worked example

The same five tasks are run against both representations in PostgreSQL. The `orders_doc` table has two columns, `id` `int` and `doc jsonb`; each document is the order with embedded customer and items, built from the normalised tables with `jsonb_build_object` and `jsonb_agg` (500,000 rows, average document size 499 bytes). A GIN index `jsonb_path_ops` and a B-tree expression index on the customer id are created on the document table. Timings are `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` execution times after one warm-up run.

#### Task 1: fetch one order with its items

blocks.code:
SELECT o.id, o.status, c.name, i.line_no, p.name, i.qty, i.unit_price
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
              JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
              JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
WHERE o.id = 250007;

-- Document: one primary key lookup
SELECT doc FROM orders_doc WHERE id = 250007;
blocks.title: Relational: four tables joined

blocks.text:
The relational plan is three nested loops over four index scans (`orders_pkey`, `customers_pkey`, `order_items_pkey`, and `products_pkey` four times) with 17 shared buffer hits and 6 reads; the execution time is 0.169 ms. The document plan is one `Index Scan using orders_doc_pkey` with 1 hit and 3 reads; the execution time is 0.049 ms. The document needs a third of the time, and the saving comes from fetching one tuple instead of seven (one order, one customer, four items, four products through a hash of repeated lookups). For a read path that serves one aggregate at a time, this is the legitimate advantage of the document model; in absolute terms both are well below a millisecond, so the benefit becomes visible only at high request rates or when the joined tables are not cached.

#### Task 2: search by attributes of the order and its items

The query counts orders from customers in Pune that contain a product of category toys.

blocks.code:
SELECT count(DISTINCT o.id)
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
              JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
              JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
WHERE c.city = 'Pune' AND p.category = 'toys';

SELECT count(*) FROM orders_doc
WHERE doc @> '{"customer":{"city":"Pune"},"items":[{"category":"toys"}]}';
blocks.title: Relational and document forms

rows: two parallel workers, seq scans of orders and order\_items
evaluates the containment on all 500,000 documents
bitmap index scan (about 10 ms) then 24,465 heap blocks to recheck
blocks.caption: Task 2: 33,250 matching orders.

blocks.text:
The GIN index finds the candidate rows in about 10 ms, but the query still reads 24,465 heap blocks, because the predicate matches 6.6 percent of the table (33,250 of 500,000 rows) and the matches are spread over nearly all pages. The index brought a factor of 2.2 over the sequential scan, not a factor of 1,000, because the predicate is not selective. A selective predicate (a customer id, an order id) is where indexes dominate; for non-selective filters the cost is the number of pages that hold results.

#### Task 3: selective lookup by a nested field

blocks.title: Customer's orders: B-tree on the relational column and an expression index on the document

blocks.text:
Both queries return 10 rows in 0.07 ms (`Bitmap Heap Scan` on `orders` in 0.074 ms, `Index Scan` on `idx_doc_cust` in 0.072 ms). A single-path B-tree index on a JSONB expression performs like an ordinary index. The expression in the query must match the expression in the index exactly, including the cast.

#### Task 4: analytics over all items

blocks.title: Revenue by category

blocks.text:
The relational query scans the narrow `order_items` table in parallel (about 125 MB of pages) and joins to the small `products` table by hash: 762 ms. The document query must read every document (all 261 MB of the table, including the document payload), expand each array with `jsonb_array_elements` (500,000 calls), extract and cast text from JSON values, and takes 2,076 ms, 2.7 times as long. This is the generic cost of analytics on a document layout: the data that the query needs is spread inside larger values, and the aggregation processes strings and casts. A column store or a relational table has no equivalent overhead. MongoDB's aggregation pipeline has the same structure (`$unwind` on items, `$group` by category) and the same character: it reads every document.

#### Task 5: update one field

blocks.title: Set the status of 20,000 orders

blocks.text: The relational update took 176 ms, the document update 833 ms (4.7 times). The cause is write amplification. The relational row is a few dozen bytes, the whole `jsonb` value about 500 bytes, and PostgreSQL writes a new version of the entire row for any change. Moreover, the document table has a GIN index over the whole value, so every update must add new index entries, and the statistics after the run show that none of the 20,000 updates were HOT updates (heap-only tuple updates that avoid index maintenance), whereas for the `orders` table the number of HOT updates was 68 of 20,000 (a likely reason for the small count is that the pages had no free space, since the table was loaded at full page density, and a HOT update needs room on the same page). In MongoDB an update of one field in a large document is likewise a rewrite of the document in the storage engine's B-tree page and an oplog entry that carries only the delta; the write-amplification argument applies to documents that are large and updated often, which is one of the reasons for the bucket and subset patterns.

blocks.text: #### Space and constraints

rows: includes copies of customer and product fields in every document
blocks.caption: Storage cost of the two layouts after loading and updating (measured).

blocks.text: The document layout needs about 1.7 times the heap space because each order repeats the customer name, city, product name and category. This is the cost of denormalisation, paid once in space and each time in keeping the copies correct. A JSONB column can regain some of the relational guarantees with constraints and generated columns. Real output:

blocks.title: Constraints on a JSONB column (PostgreSQL 16, real output)

blocks.text:
The check constraint rejects a document without a status, which is the equivalent of MongoDB `$jsonSchema` validation, and the generated column exposes a document field as an ordinary typed, indexable column with statistics, so the planner estimates it correctly (in the final run, a filter on that column returned 96,001 rows through an ordinary bitmap scan on the B-tree index).

### Hands-on

#### The MongoDB form of the five tasks

The following mongosh and Spring Data forms correspond to the tasks. They are typical, not run on the build machine.

**Document-store equivalents (typical, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.code:
// Task 1: one read
db.orders.findOne({ _id: 250007 })

// Task 2: search with a multikey compound index on the embedded fields
db.orders.createIndex({ 'customer.city': 1, 'items.category': 1 })
db.orders.countDocuments({ 'customer.city': 'Pune', 'items.category': 'toys' })

// Task 3: selective lookup
db.orders.createIndex({ 'customer.id': 1 })
db.orders.find({ 'customer.id': 5434 }, { _id: 1 })

// Task 4: analytics
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $unwind: '$items' },
  { $group: { _id: '$items.category',
              rev: { $sum: { $multiply: ['$items.qty', '$items.unitPrice'] } } } },
  { $sort: { _id: 1 } } ])

// Task 5: update one field
db.orders.updateMany({ _id: { $gte: 100001, $lte: 120000 }, status: { $ne: 'SHIPPED' } },
                     { $set: { status: 'SHIPPED' } })

blocks.text:
Two details differ from the SQL forms. The compound multikey index of task 2 contains entries for every combination of city and item category, so documents with several items produce several entries; and the `countDocuments` can be answered from the index alone only when the filter is fully covered, which a multikey path on arrays does not guarantee. In task 5, `$ne` makes the update idempotent and skips documents that are already shipped.

#### Exporting relational rows as documents

Migration to a document store often starts with generating documents from the relational data. The statement below builds the order documents (the same as in the benchmark) and writes them as newline-delimited JSON; `mongoimport` then loads them. The first two lines of the real output follow, cut for the page.

blocks.code:
$ psql shop -t -A -c "SELECT jsonb_build_object('_id', id) || doc \
    FROM orders_doc ORDER BY id LIMIT 2" | cut -c1-95
{"_id": 1, "items": [{"qty": 3, "name": "Product 49", "category": "electronics", "productId": 4
{"_id": 2, "items": [{"qty": 4, "name": "Product 80", "category": "grocery", "productId": 80, "
blocks.title: Generating NDJSON from PostgreSQL (real output, each line cut to 95 characters)

blocks.code:
psql shop -t -A -c "SELECT jsonb_build_object('_id', id) || doc FROM orders_doc" > orders.ndjson
mongoimport --uri "mongodb://db1:27017/shop" --collection orders --file orders.ndjson
blocks.title: Loading the documents into MongoDB (typical, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
Two conversions need care. JSON numbers lose the distinction between integers and decimals: `833.00` becomes a double, so monetary values should be converted to Decimal128 (`$convert`) or stored as integer minor units. Timestamps arrive as strings and must be converted to BSON dates (`$toDate` in an update pipeline, or the extended JSON form `{"$date": "..."}` in the export).

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Incident: document store used for relational data

**Scenario.** A team picks MongoDB for a reporting product because "the schema will change a lot". Customers, orders, invoices and payments become separate collections with ids referencing each other, and the application joins them in Java code.

**Symptoms.** Endpoints issue dozens of queries; the service holds large lists in memory to join them; reports are inconsistent when two collections are read at different moments; a bug leaves orphaned invoices because no constraint exists.

**Diagnosis.** Count queries per request (profiler or driver command listener). Look for `find` calls on one collection driven by the ids in the result of another. Review the schema: collections with many references and no embedded data are relational data in a document store.

**Root cause.** The data is highly connected and queried across entity boundaries, the access pattern that relational databases are designed for. The document model rewards aggregates read as a unit; here no such unit exists.

**Fix.** Immediate: cache reference data and batch lookups with `$in` or `$lookup` to cut round trips. Permanent: either redesign the hot read paths as aggregates (embed what is read together, copy display data) or move the connected data to PostgreSQL, keeping MongoDB for the document-shaped parts. A migration follows the staged procedure described below.

**Prevention.** Decide the model from the list of queries and invariants, not from the expected rate of schema change; JSONB or `$jsonSchema` handle schema change in either world.

#### Incident: JSONB column used as a catch-all

**Scenario.** To avoid schema migrations, all product attributes are stored in one `jsonb` column of the `products` table, including price and stock, which are updated frequently and used in joins.

**Symptoms.** Updates of stock become slow and the table bloats; queries on price filters are mis-estimated by the planner (the plan flips between nested loop and hash join); reports require casts everywhere; occasionally a string appears where a number was expected.

**Diagnosis.** `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` shows estimated rows far from actual rows for predicates on JSON paths (the planner has no statistics inside the value); `pg_stat_user_tables` shows many updates without HOT updates and a growing `n_dead_tup`; `SELECT DISTINCT jsonb_typeof(attrs->'price') FROM products` returns more than one type.

**Root cause.** Frequently updated, constrained, relational attributes were put in a structure that rewrites the whole value, has no column statistics and no type enforcement.

**Fix.** Immediate: add generated columns (`price numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS ((attrs->>'price')::numeric)` `STORED`) with B-tree indexes, and a `CHECK` constraint on the type. Permanent: move stable, queried, updated attributes to real columns and keep only the variable long tail (colour, size, material, vendor-specific keys) in `jsonb`. **Prevention.** Rule of thumb: a field that appears in a `WHERE`, `JOIN`, `ORDER BY` or `UPDATE` of a hot path belongs in a column.

#### Incident: premature sharding or premature NoSQL for scale

**Scenario.** A start-up chooses a sharded MongoDB cluster for a service that stores 20 GB and handles 300 requests per second, "to be ready for scale".

**Symptoms.** Operations cost three shards, three config servers and routers; development slows because of shard-key constraints (unique indexes, targeted queries); a scatter-gather query is slower than the same query on one node would be.

**Diagnosis.** Compare the actual load with single-node capacity: 20 GB fits in the memory of a modest server, and a single PostgreSQL or MongoDB replica set handles thousands of simple operations per second.

**Root cause.** Scale-out machinery was adopted for a hypothetical load, with its constraints paid immediately.

**Fix.** Collapse to a replica set (a single primary with replicas); defer sharding until measurements show a limit that vertical scaling, indexing, caching and read replicas cannot meet.

**Prevention.** Document the capacity thresholds that trigger a re-architecture and review them against measured load every quarter.

### When to choose which

#### Decision rules

The rules below apply in order; the first that matches decides.

1. The data has strong cross-entity invariants (balances, inventory, uniqueness across entities) or needs ad hoc joins and reporting: choose a relational database.
2. The unit of work is one self-contained aggregate (a product page, a user profile, a shopping cart, an event) read and written as a whole, and its shape varies between records: a document store fits; embed what is read together.
3. Write throughput or data volume exceeds one primary and the access path has a natural partition key (customer, device, tenant): a sharded document store, or a partitioned relational database, fits.
4. The data is mostly relational with a variable tail of attributes: PostgreSQL with `jsonb` for the tail.
5. Otherwise choose the technology the team operates well; the operational cost of an unfamiliar database often exceeds the gain of a better data model.

blocks.text:
#### Hybrid architectures

A single system often uses both. The relational database is the system of record for orders, payments and inventory, where constraints and transactions matter. MongoDB stores documents that are read as a whole and tolerate eventual consistency: the product catalogue with variable attributes, a denormalised order history view for the customer-facing app, and an append-only event log. The two are kept in step through the outbox pattern: the service writes the order and an outbox row in one relational transaction; a relay publishes the outbox rows to a message broker or writes them to MongoDB idempotently (the `_id` of the document is the id of the outbox row, so a repeated delivery overwrites instead of duplicating). Reads of the history view go to MongoDB; writes that must be consistent go to PostgreSQL.

#### Migrating between them

A migration is a sequence of reversible stages, each deployed and observed separately.

blocks.text:
1. **Model.** Derive the target from the query list. Relational to document: pick the aggregate root, embed the child rows read with it, copy display fields, keep references for shared entities. Document to relational: map each embedded array to a child table with a foreign key and extract the stable fields to typed columns.
2. **Dual write.** The application writes to both stores; the old store remains authoritative, and a failure to write the new store is logged and queued, not surfaced to the user.
3. **Backfill.** A batch job copies history in key order with checkpoints; every copy is an idempotent upsert (`_id` or primary key preserved).
4. **Verify.** Compare counts per key range and checksums of selected fields; run shadow reads that query both stores and diff the responses.
5. **Switch reads.** Move endpoints one at a time behind a feature flag, starting with low-risk ones, watching latency and error rates.
6. **Retire.** Stop writing to the old store after a rollback window, then archive it.

The most common errors are copying `_id` or key values inconsistently, converting decimals and dates through floating point or strings, and skipping the verification stage.

### Questions to expect

#### Questions and model answers

1. **When would you choose MongoDB over PostgreSQL?** When the unit of access is a self-contained aggregate with varying shape, when horizontal write scale through sharding is required, or when documents map naturally onto application objects. For relational integrity, joins and reporting, PostgreSQL.
2. **Can PostgreSQL replace a document database?** For many workloads yes: `jsonb` with GIN and expression indexes, constraints and transactions cover flexible attributes. It does not provide built-in sharding with automatic balancing, and whole-value rewrites make large frequently updated documents expensive.
3. **What does denormalisation cost?** Space, and the work of keeping copies consistent: updating shared data (a customer's city) means updating every copy or accepting staleness, which is acceptable only where the copy is a historical snapshot.
4. **Why was the analytic query slower on JSONB in the benchmark?** It had to read every document, expand arrays and cast text values; the normalised layout scans a narrow table of typed columns.
5. **Why did the GIN index help only moderately in task 2?** The predicate matched 6.6 percent of the rows spread over almost all pages; the index finds them quickly but the heap pages still have to be read.
6. **How does a transaction across entities differ in the two systems?** PostgreSQL treats it as the ordinary case; MongoDB prefers to make it a single-document write and offers bounded multi-document transactions (60 second limit, snapshot isolation).
7. **What is the outbox pattern?** Writing the business change and an event row in one local transaction and publishing the event later, so that two stores stay consistent without a distributed transaction.
8. **How do you migrate with no downtime?** Dual writes, idempotent backfill, verification, gradual switch of reads, then retirement of the old store, with a rollback path at every stage.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Choose by access pattern and invariants, then verify with measurements on your own data.

- Document layouts win single-aggregate reads (here 0.049 ms against 0.169 ms); normalised layouts win analytics (762 ms against 2,076 ms) and small updates (176 ms against 833 ms).
- JSONB is a good home for the variable tail of attributes; keep queried and frequently updated fields in typed columns.
- A GIN index helps selective containment queries; a non-selective predicate remains bounded by the pages that hold the result.
- Sharding and NoSQL adopted for hypothetical scale cost complexity immediately; migrate in reversible stages when it is justified.

The questions below are grouped by topic and cover the full book. Each answer is a model answer of two to five lines: the points an interviewer expects, in the order in which they should be stated. A strong candidate adds one concrete example (a query, a plan node, a configuration key) and names the trade-off. The scenario questions at the end combine several topics and are answered as a diagnosis procedure. The answers state PostgreSQL behaviour as observed in PostgreSQL 16 and MySQL and MongoDB behaviour as documented for MySQL 8.x and MongoDB 7.x and 8.x.

### DBMS basics

#### Questions 1 to 10

1. **What is a DBMS and what does it provide beyond files?** Software that stores data and provides a query language, concurrency control, transactions, recovery after failure, access control and integrity constraints. A file system provides none of these; each application would need to implement them.
2. **What is the three-schema architecture?** External schemas (views per user group), the conceptual schema (the logical structure of the whole database) and the internal schema (physical storage). It gives logical data independence (changing the conceptual schema without breaking views) and physical data independence (changing storage without changing the logical schema).
3. **What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?** OLTP serves many short transactions that read and write a few rows by key (orders, payments) and favours row storage and indexes. OLAP runs few long queries that scan and aggregate many rows and favours column storage and parallel scans.
4. **What is the difference between a primary key, a candidate key and a super key?** A super key is any set of attributes that identifies a row; a candidate key is a minimal super key; the primary key is the candidate key chosen as the main identifier. Remaining candidate keys become unique constraints.
5. **Surrogate or natural key?** A surrogate key (identity, UUID) is stable and compact and does not change when business data changes. A natural key (email, ISBN) has meaning but can change or be reused. Common practice is a surrogate primary key plus a unique constraint on the natural key.
6. **What integrity constraints exist?** Domain (type, CHECK), NOT NULL, entity integrity (primary key), referential integrity (foreign key) and UNIQUE. Constraints put the rule in the database so that every application is subject to it.
7. **What is a foreign key and what do the referential actions do?** A column that references a key in another table. On delete or update of the parent, `RESTRICT` and `NO ACTION` reject, `CASCADE` propagates, `SET NULL` and `SET` `DEFAULT` replace the value.
8. **What is NULL and how does it behave in comparisons?** NULL means unknown. Comparisons with NULL yield unknown (three-valued logic), so `x = NULL` is never true; use `IS NULL`. `WHERE` keeps only rows where the predicate is true, and `NOT IN` with a NULL in the list returns no rows.
9. **What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?** `DELETE` removes selected rows, is logged per row and can be rolled back; `TRUNCATE` removes all rows quickly by deallocating storage (transactional in PostgreSQL, implicit commit in MySQL); `DROP` removes the table definition too.
10. **What is a view and what is a materialised view?** A view is a stored query evaluated at each use. A materialised view stores the result and must be refreshed (`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`), trading freshness for speed.

### SQL

#### Questions 11 to 22

1. **In which order does SQL logically process a SELECT?** FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT (including window functions), DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. This explains why a select alias cannot be used in WHERE but can be used in ORDER BY.
2. **What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?** `WHERE` filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation.
3. **Explain the join types.** Inner returns matching pairs; left (right) keeps all rows of one side with NULLs where no match exists; full keeps both; cross returns the Cartesian product; a self join joins a table to itself; semi and anti joins (`EXISTS`, `NOT EXISTS`) test for existence of matches without returning columns of the other side.
4. **What is the difference between a filter in ON and in WHERE for a left join?** A condition on the right table in `WHERE` removes the NULL-extended rows and turns the join into an inner join; in `ON` it restricts which rows match while keeping all left rows.
5. **What is the difference between the three COUNT forms?** `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values; `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts distinct non-NULL values.
6. **How do you find the second highest salary?** `SELECT max(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT` `max(salary) FROM emp)`, or `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)` and filter on rank 2, which also handles ties and the Nth case.
7. **How do you find duplicate rows?** `SELECT col, count(*) FROM t GROUP BY col HAVING count(*) > 1`; to delete duplicates keep one row per group with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY col ORDER BY id)` and delete rows with number above 1.
8. **What is a window function and how does it differ from GROUP BY?** It computes a value over a set of related rows without collapsing them, so each input row stays in the output. Examples: `ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, `LAG`, `SUM() OVER` `(ORDER BY ...)` for running totals.
9. **ROW\_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE\_RANK?** `ROW_NUMBER` gives unique consecutive numbers; `RANK` gives ties the same rank and leaves gaps after them; `DENSE_RANK` gives ties the same rank with no gaps.
10. **What is a CTE and what is a recursive CTE?** A named subquery (`WITH`) used for readability and reuse. A recursive CTE has an anchor and a recursive member joined by `UNION ALL` and walks hierarchies such as organisation trees; a termination condition or a depth limit prevents endless recursion.
11. **EXISTS or IN?** They are logically equivalent for non-NULL values and the optimiser usually produces the same semi-join plan. `NOT IN` differs from `NOT EXISTS` when the subquery can return NULL: `NOT IN` then returns nothing, so `NOT EXISTS` is the safe form.
12. **What is an upsert?** Insert or update in one statement: PostgreSQL `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE`, MySQL `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`. It is atomic and avoids the race of select-then-insert.

### Normalisation and modelling

#### Questions 23 to 30

1. **What is normalisation and why is it done?** Structuring tables so that each fact is stored once, to avoid insertion, update and deletion anomalies. It is based on functional dependencies.
2. **State 1NF, 2NF and 3NF.** 1NF: atomic values and no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF and no non-key attribute depends on part of a composite key. 3NF: 2NF and no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (no transitive dependency).
3. **What is BCNF and how does it differ from 3NF?** In BCNF every determinant of a non-trivial functional dependency is a super key. 3NF allows a dependency whose right side is a prime attribute; BCNF does not, and a BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation.
4. **What are update, insertion and deletion anomalies?** Redundant copies get out of step on update; a fact cannot be stored without an unrelated fact on insertion; deleting a row destroys an unrelated fact.
5. **When would you denormalise?** When measured read cost of joins is a problem and the duplicated data changes rarely or is a historical snapshot (price at order time); the price is extra writes and the risk of inconsistency, managed by triggers, application logic or periodic reconciliation.
6. **How is a many-to-many relationship modelled?** With an association table holding the foreign keys of both sides as a composite primary key, plus attributes of the relationship (quantity, date).
7. **What is a weak entity?** An entity without its own key, identified through an owner entity (order line identified by order id and line number); it is implemented with a composite key containing the owner's key.
8. **What is a lossless decomposition?** A decomposition whose natural join of the parts reproduces the original table exactly, with no spurious tuples. It holds when the common attributes form a key of one of the parts.

### Indexes and query performance

#### Questions 31 to 42

1. **What is an index and what does it cost?** An auxiliary structure (usually a B+tree) mapping key values to row locations so that lookups avoid a full scan. It costs space and slows writes, because every insert, update of an indexed column and delete maintains each index.
2. **How does a B+tree index work?** Balanced tree with internal nodes holding separator keys and leaf nodes holding keys with row pointers, leaves linked in key order. A lookup descends from the root in a few page reads (typically three or four levels for millions of rows) and range scans follow the leaf links.
3. **What is the leftmost prefix rule for composite indexes?** An index on (a, b, c) serves filters on a, on a and b, and on a, b and c; it does not serve a filter on b alone. Equality columns come first, then the range or sort column.
4. **What is a covering index?** An index that contains all columns a query needs (with `INCLUDE` in PostgreSQL), so the query is answered by an index-only scan without visiting the table, provided the visibility map shows the pages as all-visible.
5. **When is an index not used?** When the predicate is not sargable (a function on the column, `LIKE '%x'`, an implicit cast), when the predicate matches a large fraction of the table, when statistics are stale, or when the table is small. The fix depends on the cause: expression index, rewrite, `ANALYZE`, or none.
6. **What is selectivity and cardinality?** Cardinality is the number of distinct values; selectivity is the fraction of rows a predicate returns. Indexes pay off for low fractions (high selectivity in the sense of few rows).
7. **What do Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan and Bitmap Heap Scan mean?** Read the whole table; walk the index and fetch each row; answer from the index alone; collect matching row locations from one or more indexes into a bitmap and read the heap pages in physical order, which suits mid-sized result sets.
8. **How do you read EXPLAIN ANALYZE?** Compare estimated rows with actual rows at each node (a large mismatch points to stale statistics), look at `actual time`, `loops` (multiply per-loop time by loops), buffers (`shared` `hit` and `read`), and rows removed by filter. The most expensive node by actual time is the starting point.
9. **Nested loop, hash join and merge join?** Nested loop probes the inner side per outer row, best with an index and few outer rows; hash join builds a hash table on one input, good for large unsorted inputs; merge join merges two sorted inputs and is good when both are already sorted.
10. **Why is OFFSET pagination slow for deep pages?** The server must produce and discard all skipped rows. Keyset pagination (`WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n`) uses an index seek and has constant cost.
11. **What is the N+1 query problem?** Loading N parents and then issuing one query per parent for a lazy association: N+1 statements. Fix with `JOIN FETCH`, entity graphs, batch fetching (`@BatchSize`) or a projection query.
12. **How do you find slow queries in production?** `pg_stat_statements` (total and mean time per normalised query), `log_min_duration_statement`, `auto_explain` for plans, and the MySQL slow query log with `performance_schema`; then `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the worst offenders.

### Transactions and isolation

#### Questions 43 to 52

1. **What does ACID mean?** Atomicity (all or nothing), consistency (constraints hold before and after), isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work) and durability (committed data survives a crash, via the write-ahead log).
2. **Name the concurrency anomalies.** Dirty read (reading uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (a row read twice changes), phantom read (a repeated query returns new rows), lost update (two read-modify-write cycles overwrite each other) and write skew (two transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint rows, breaking an invariant).
3. **What are the SQL isolation levels?** Read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read and serializable, each forbidding more anomalies. PostgreSQL treats read uncommitted as read committed and its repeatable read as snapshot isolation.
4. **What are the defaults in PostgreSQL and MySQL?** PostgreSQL: read committed. MySQL InnoDB: repeatable read, with next-key locks that prevent most phantoms.
5. **How does PostgreSQL implement serializable?** Serializable snapshot isolation: snapshot reads plus detection of dangerous read-write dependency cycles, aborting one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001, which the application must retry.
6. **How do you prevent a lost update?** An atomic update (`SET qty = qty - 1`), `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, optimistic locking with a version column, or a higher isolation level with retry.
7. **What is optimistic versus pessimistic locking?** Pessimistic locks the row when reading (`FOR UPDATE`) and blocks others; optimistic reads without locking and checks at update time that the version has not changed, retrying on conflict. Optimistic suits low contention.
8. **What is a deadlock and how is it handled?** Two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds. The database detects the cycle and aborts one (PostgreSQL after `deadlock_timeout`, 1 s by default). Prevent by locking rows in a consistent order and keeping transactions short.
9. **What do** `SKIP LOCKED` **and** `NOWAIT` **do?** `NOWAIT` fails at once if the row is locked; `SKIP LOCKED` skips locked rows, which allows several workers to take jobs from a queue table without blocking each other.
10. **What is a savepoint?** A named point inside a transaction to which part of the work can be rolled back without aborting the whole transaction (`SAVEPOINT`, `ROLLBACK TO`).

### MVCC, WAL and recovery

#### Questions 53 to 60

1. **What is MVCC?** Multi-version concurrency control: writers create new row versions while readers continue to see the version that was current for their snapshot, so readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers.
2. **How does PostgreSQL store versions?** Each tuple has `xmin` (creating transaction) and `xmax` (deleting or locking transaction); an update marks the old tuple with `xmax` and inserts a new tuple. A snapshot decides visibility from these ids and the commit status.
3. **How does InnoDB differ?** It updates the row in place in the clustered index and keeps old versions in undo logs; a read view reconstructs old versions from the undo chain. There is no heap bloat but long transactions grow the undo history.
4. **What is VACUUM and why is it needed?** It removes dead tuples that no snapshot can see, updates the visibility map and free space map, and freezes old transaction ids. Without it tables bloat and transaction id wraparound approaches.
5. **What is transaction id wraparound?** Transaction ids are 32 bits and compared modulo 2^32; if old rows are not frozen, they appear to be in the future and become invisible. PostgreSQL warns and finally refuses writes to protect data; anti-wraparound autovacuum prevents it.
6. **What is the write-ahead log?** Changes are first appended to a sequential log and flushed at commit; data pages are written later. After a crash the log is replayed (redo) to restore committed changes, so durability needs one sequential flush instead of random page writes.
7. **What is a checkpoint?** A point at which all dirty pages are flushed so that recovery needs to replay only the WAL after it; checkpoint frequency trades recovery time against write bursts.
8. **What does** `synchronous_commit` **control?** Whether a commit waits for the WAL flush (and, with synchronous replication, for the standby). Turning it off can lose the last few commits on a crash but never corrupts the database.

### PostgreSQL and MySQL differences

#### Questions 61 to 68

1. **How are rows stored in PostgreSQL and in InnoDB?** PostgreSQL stores rows in an unordered heap with all indexes secondary; InnoDB stores rows in the clustered primary key B+tree, and secondary indexes hold the primary key value, so a secondary lookup needs a second tree descent.
2. **What follows from the clustered index for primary key choice?** In InnoDB a large or random primary key (a random UUID) enlarges every secondary index and causes page splits; a short monotonic key is preferred. In PostgreSQL the key size affects only the index itself.
3. **How do auto-increment columns differ?** PostgreSQL uses sequences (`GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY`) that are not rolled back, so gaps appear; MySQL uses `AUTO_INCREMENT` per table with similar gaps after rollback or failed inserts.
4. **What type differences matter?** PostgreSQL has `timestamptz`, arrays, `jsonb`, native `boolean` and `uuid`; MySQL has `DATETIME` and `TIMESTAMP` (with its range limit and time zone conversion) and `JSON`. Both treat empty string and NULL differently from Oracle.
5. **How do DDL and locking differ?** Most PostgreSQL DDL is transactional; MySQL DDL commits implicitly. Adding a column with a constant default is instant in PostgreSQL 11 and later and MySQL 8 uses instant algorithms for many changes; both can still take locks that queue behind long transactions.
6. **How do replication mechanisms compare?** PostgreSQL streams WAL (physical) or uses logical replication; MySQL replicates the binary log (statement, row or mixed) and supports group replication and semi-synchronous modes.
7. **Which has better JSON support?** PostgreSQL `jsonb` has GIN indexing and a rich path language; MySQL `JSON` has generated-column and multi-valued indexes. Both are adequate for a variable tail of attributes.
8. **What is a PostgreSQL feature with no direct MySQL equivalent?** Partial indexes, `RETURNING`, rich index types (GIN, GiST, BRIN), `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, extensions such as PostGIS; MySQL has no partial indexes and had no `RETURNING` for inserts (MariaDB does).

### Scaling, replication and sharding

#### Questions 69 to 78

1. **Why use a connection pool?** Opening a database connection is expensive (a process in PostgreSQL) and the server supports a limited number. A pool such as HikariCP reuses connections and bounds concurrency; its size should be small (roughly cores times two plus disks), not equal to the number of request threads.
2. **What happens when the pool is exhausted?** Threads wait for a connection up to `connectionTimeout` and then fail. Common causes are transactions that stay open while calling remote services and queries that are too slow.
3. **What is replication lag and why does it matter?** Asynchronous replicas apply changes after the primary, so reads from them can be stale. Read-your-writes flows must read from the primary or wait for the replica to pass a known position.
4. **Synchronous versus asynchronous replication?** Synchronous waits for the standby before commit (no loss of acknowledged data, higher latency, availability depends on the standby); asynchronous does not wait (low latency, possible loss on failover).
5. **What is split brain?** Two nodes both act as primary after a network partition and accept divergent writes. Prevent with quorum, fencing and a consensus-backed failover manager.
6. **Partitioning versus sharding?** Partitioning splits a table into parts inside one database server (pruning, maintenance); sharding distributes data across independent servers, each holding a subset, with routing and cross-shard limits.
7. **What makes a good shard key?** High cardinality, even frequency, no monotonic growth, and presence in common queries; hashed keys spread load, ranged keys support range queries.
8. **What is consistent hashing?** Keys and nodes are mapped onto a ring and a key belongs to the next node clockwise; adding or removing a node moves only the keys of one neighbour, and virtual nodes smooth the distribution.
9. **How do you take a backup that you can trust?** Physical base backup plus archived WAL for point-in-time recovery, or logical dumps for small data, and, above all, a regular restore test that measures the real recovery time.
10. **What are RPO and RTO?** Recovery point objective: the maximum acceptable data loss in time. Recovery time objective: the maximum acceptable time to restore service.

### NoSQL and the CAP theorem

#### Questions 79 to 88

1. **Why NoSQL?** Horizontal scale, flexible schema, and data models matched to access patterns (documents, key-value, wide-column, graph), accepting weaker joins or transactions. The name does not mean the absence of SQL.
2. **State the CAP theorem precisely.** In the presence of a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency (linearizability) and availability (every non-failing node answers). Without a partition both are possible; CAP does not say "pick two of three".
3. **What does PACELC add?** If there is a partition, choose availability or consistency; else (normal operation) choose between latency and consistency. It captures the latency cost of strong consistency.
4. **What is eventual consistency?** If no new updates are made, all replicas converge to the same value eventually. Between updates readers can see stale data.
5. **What is quorum replication?** With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read queries R replicas; if R + W \> N, every read set overlaps the latest write set, so the latest acknowledged write is visible to the read.
6. **What are vector clocks and last-write-wins?** A vector clock records the causal history of each version so concurrent versions can be detected and merged; last-write-wins keeps the version with the highest timestamp, which silently drops concurrent updates and depends on clock accuracy.
7. **What is the difference between a B-tree and an LSM-tree storage engine?** B-trees update pages in place and read with few I/Os; LSM-trees buffer writes in memory, flush sorted immutable files and merge them by compaction, giving high write throughput at the cost of read and space amplification.
8. **What is a tombstone and why can it hurt?** A delete marker in LSM-based stores; the data is removed only at compaction, and reads must skip accumulated tombstones, which slows queries on frequently deleted partitions.
9. **When is a graph database better than relational?** For queries that traverse many relationships of variable depth (friends of friends, fraud rings); each hop is an index-free adjacency step instead of a join, whereas a relational recursive query repeats joins.
10. **What is polyglot persistence?** Using several database types in one system, each for the data it fits, for example PostgreSQL for orders, a document store for catalogue, a search engine for text and a cache for hot reads.

### MongoDB

#### Questions 89 to 100

1. **What is the document model?** Data stored as BSON documents (nested fields, arrays, rich types) in collections without a fixed schema; related data is embedded in one document when it is read and changed together.
2. **When do you embed and when do you reference?** Embed for one-to-few relationships read with the parent and bounded in size; reference for large or unbounded children, data shared by many parents, or data updated independently. Unbounded arrays must be avoided (16 MB document limit).
3. **What is the aggregation pipeline?** A sequence of stages (`$match`, `$group`, `$sort`, `$lookup`, `$unwind`, `$project`) in which each stage transforms the document stream; `$match` and `$sort` early use indexes and reduce work.
4. **What is the ESR rule?** For compound indexes order fields as Equality, Sort, Range, so equality filters narrow the scan, the sort uses the index order, and the range is applied last.
5. **How do you read** `explain('executionStats')`**?** Compare `nReturned`, `totalKeysExamined` and `totalDocsExamined`; a large ratio of examined to returned documents or a `COLLSCAN` stage indicates a missing or poorly ordered index.
6. **How does MongoDB provide atomicity?** A single-document write is atomic; multi-document transactions provide snapshot isolation on replica sets and sharded clusters, with a 60-second default limit.
7. **What is a replica set and how does failover work?** Members replicate the primary's oplog; if the primary is unreachable for the election timeout (10 s by default) the secondaries elect a new primary by majority vote in a higher term, typically within about 12 seconds.
8. **What are write concern, read concern and read preference?** Write concern: how many members must acknowledge a write (`w: majority` survives failover). Read concern: the consistency level of returned data (`majority`, `snapshot`). Read preference: which member serves reads.
9. **How does sharding work in MongoDB?** A shard key partitions data into chunks assigned to shards (replica sets); mongos routes by the chunk map from the config servers; the balancer migrates chunks to even out data.
10. **What causes a hot shard and a jumbo chunk?** A hot shard comes from a monotonic or skewed key sending most writes to one chunk; a jumbo chunk from a key with too few distinct values so that a chunk cannot be split.
11. **What is the oplog?** A capped collection of idempotent operations on the primary, tailed by secondaries; its size determines how long a secondary may be offline before it needs a full resync.
12. **What is NoSQL injection?** Operator objects in user input (`{"$ne": null}`) change the meaning of a query. Prevent with typed request objects and validation instead of passing raw maps into queries.

### Spring and JPA data access

#### Questions 101 to 110

1. **What does** `@Transactional` **do?** A proxy starts a transaction before the method, commits on normal return and rolls back on a runtime exception (not on checked exceptions by default). It works only on calls that pass through the proxy.
2. **Why does** `@Transactional` **sometimes not apply?** Self-invocation within the same class, a non-public or final method, a missing transaction manager (for MongoDB it must be declared), or a swallowed exception.
3. **What are the propagation types?** `REQUIRED` (join or start), `REQUIRES_NEW` (suspend and start a new one), `SUPPORTS`, `MANDATORY`, `NEVER`, `NOT_SUPPORTED` and `NESTED` (savepoint). `REQUIRES_NEW` holds a second connection, which can exhaust a pool.
4. **Lazy versus eager loading in JPA?** Lazy fetches an association on first access, eager with the parent. Lazy access outside the session raises `LazyInitializationException`; both can cause N+1 queries when used in loops.
5. **How do you fix N+1 in JPA?** `JOIN FETCH` in JPQL, `@EntityGraph`, `@BatchSize` or `default_batch_fetch_size`, or a DTO projection that selects the needed columns in one query.
6. **What does** `open-in-view` **do?** It keeps the persistence context open during web view rendering, hiding lazy loading problems and holding a connection longer; production configurations usually disable it (`spring.jpa.open-in-view=false`).
7. **How does optimistic locking work in JPA?** A `@Version` field is included in the `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND` `version = ?`; zero affected rows raises `OptimisticLockException`, which the application retries.
8. **What does a HikariCP pool need configured?** `maximumPoolSize` (small), `connectionTimeout`, `maxLifetime` (below any database or proxy timeout), `idleTimeout`, and leak detection (`leakDetectionThreshold`) during diagnosis.
9. **How do you prevent SQL injection in JDBC?** Use `PreparedStatement` parameters (or JPA parameters) so values are never concatenated into the SQL text; whitelist dynamic identifiers such as sort columns.
10. **How does Flyway work?** It applies versioned SQL migrations in order, recording them in a history table with checksums; changed applied migrations fail validation. Zero-downtime changes use expand and contract: add, migrate data, switch code, remove.

### Scenario questions

#### Questions 111 to 120

1. **An endpoint became slow after a release. What do you do first?** Identify the query (slow query log, `pg_stat_statements`), run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, compare estimates with actuals, check for a new query pattern (N+1) and for a missing index or changed plan; fix and verify with the same measurement.
2. **The database CPU is at 100 percent. Where do you look?** Top queries by total time, sequential scans of large tables, a sudden increase in executions (a loop or a cache failure), missing indexes, connection storms; then act on the heaviest query.
3. **Two users bought the last item. Why and how do you fix it?** A read-check-write race (lost update). Use an atomic conditional update (`UPDATE ... SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0`) and check the affected row count, or `SELECT FOR UPDATE`.
4. **Disk usage grows quickly though data volume is stable. What are the suspects?** Table bloat from long transactions blocking vacuum, an inactive replication slot retaining WAL, a growing log or temporary files, or index bloat.
5. **Application threads hang waiting for a connection. How do you diagnose?** Check pool metrics and `pg_stat_activity` for `idle in transaction` sessions and long queries; look for transactions open across remote calls; fix the transaction boundary and add timeouts (`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`).
6. **A migration that adds an index blocked production. What happened?** A plain `CREATE INDEX` blocks writes for its duration; use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. Also, a DDL statement waiting on a long transaction queues all later queries behind its lock; set `lock_timeout`.
7. **Reads from a replica return old data after a write. How do you fix it?** Route read-after-write requests to the primary, or use causal consistency (MongoDB sessions, PostgreSQL LSN waiting), or bound staleness and show the user the pending state.
8. **A report shows different totals each run. Why?** Reading in read committed while data changes, a join fan-out duplicating rows, or non-deterministic pagination; run in a repeatable read snapshot, check join cardinality and add a unique ordering.
9. **How would you design the data layer for an order system with search and an activity feed?** PostgreSQL for orders, items, payments and inventory with constraints and transactions; an outbox feeding a search index and a MongoDB event log; a cache for product pages; replicas for reporting.
10. **What do you do when a primary fails in a three-node set?** Confirm the election result and the new primary, check that applications reconnect (retryable writes, timeouts), examine the former primary for rollback data once it returns, review replication lag and write concern effects, and record the timeline.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The bank is a revision tool: state the answer, give an example, name the trade-off.

- Basics and SQL questions test precision of definitions; index and plan questions test the ability to read evidence.
- Isolation, MVCC and recovery answers should name the mechanism, not only the property.
- Scaling and NoSQL answers should state the guarantee and the failure it prevents.
- Scenario answers are procedures: observe, narrow, fix, verify, prevent.

The tables and listings in this chapter condense the book into reference form: SQL syntax, a command map between PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB, the isolation matrix, an index decision table, a guide to reading EXPLAIN output and a mongosh crib. They state facts for PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8.x and MongoDB 7.x and 8.x, and each entry points back to the chapter that explains the mechanism.

### SQL syntax

blocks.code:
-- DDL
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,   -- MySQL: BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT
  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  status      text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW' CHECK (status IN ('NEW','PAID','SHIPPED')),
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()                  -- MySQL: DATETIME or TIMESTAMP
);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_cust ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

-- DML
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id) VALUES (5434) RETURNING id;      -- MySQL: LAST_INSERT_ID()
INSERT INTO stock (sku, qty) VALUES ('A-100', 5)
  ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty;  -- MySQL: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 2 WHERE sku = 'A-100' AND qty >= 2;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'CANCELLED' AND created_at < now() - interval '1 year';

-- Query
SELECT c.city, count(*) AS orders, sum(o.total) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'PAID') AS paid
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at >= date '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY c.city HAVING count(*) > 100
ORDER BY orders DESC LIMIT 10;

-- Window and CTE
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT o.*, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders o)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;                                -- latest 3 orders per customer

-- Locking reads and queues
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE state = 'READY' ORDER BY id
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10;

-- Transaction
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;   -- MySQL: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL ..
COMMIT;

rows: Reads the whole table; acceptable for small tables or when most rows are needed
Walks the index and fetches rows; good for few rows

blocks.caption: Plan nodes and what they imply (PostgreSQL).

blocks.text:
The checklist for a plan: first compare `rows=` (estimate) with `actual rows=` at every node, because a factor of ten or more points to stale statistics or correlated columns (`ANALYZE`, extended statistics). Second, multiply `actual time` by `loops`. Third, read `Buffers: shared hit` and `read` to see cache behaviour. Fourth, look at `Rows Removed by Filter`: a large number means the index does not match the predicate. In MongoDB the corresponding checks are `COLLSCAN` versus `IXSCAN` and the ratios `totalDocsExamined` to `nReturned` and `totalKeysExamined` to `nReturned`.

### mongosh crib

**mongosh quick reference**

blocks.code:
use shop                                         // switch database
db.orders.insertOne({ _id: 1, status: 'NEW', items: [] })
db.orders.find({ status: 'NEW', 'items.sku': 'A-100' }, { status: 1 }).sort({ _id: -1 }).limit(5)
db.orders.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { $set: { status: 'PAID' }, $inc: { version: 1 } })
db.orders.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { $push: { items: { sku: 'B-205', qty: 1 } } })
db.orders.updateOne({ _id: 1, 'items.sku': 'B-205' }, { $inc: { 'items.$.qty': 1 } })
db.orders.updateOne({ sku: 'X' }, { $setOnInsert: { qty: 0 } }, { upsert: true })
db.orders.findOneAndUpdate({ _id: 1, status: 'NEW' }, { $set: { status: 'PAID' } },
                           { returnDocument: 'after' })
db.orders.deleteMany({ status: 'CANCELLED' })
db.orders.aggregate([ { $match: { status: 'PAID' } },
  { $group: { _id: '$customerId', revenue: { $sum: '$total' } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } }, { $limit: 10 } ])
db.orders.createIndex({ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 })     // equality first, then sort/range
db.orders.createIndex({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 86400 })   // TTL
db.orders.find({ customerId: 5434 }).explain('executionStats')
db.orders.getIndexes();  db.orders.stats();  db.orders.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }])
const s = db.getMongo().startSession(); s.startTransaction({ writeConcern: { w: 'majority' } })
rs.status();  rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo();  rs.stepDown(60)
sh.status();  sh.shardCollection('shop.orders', { customerId: 'hashed' })
db.currentOp({ active: true, secs_running: { $gt: 5 } });  db.killOp(opid)
db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 100 });  db.system.profile.find().sort({ ts: -1 }).limit(5)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Reference tables help recall, not understanding; each row refers to a chapter that explains why.

- The isolation matrix differs between engines: PostgreSQL repeatable read is snapshot isolation, MySQL repeatable read is not.
- Choose an index from the query shape: equality columns first, then sort, then range.
- Read every plan by comparing estimated and actual rows before anything else.

The plan assumes about two hours on weekdays and four hours on one weekend day, which is 14 to 16 hours per week. Each week has a theme, chapters to read by name, labs that must be executed (reading output is not a substitute for running it), and a checkpoint of interview questions from the question bank that must be answered aloud without notes. A week is complete when the checkpoint answers are correct and the labs produce the documented results on the learner's own machine.

blocks.text: ### The six weeks

rows: Data and DBMS; The relational model; Entity-relationship modelling; Normalisation; Schema design and DDL
Install PostgreSQL 16 with initdb; model the e-commerce schema; reproduce an update anomaly and fix it by normalising
SQL fundamentals; Joins; Aggregation; Subqueries and CTEs; Window functions; the 30 interview SQL problems
Load the sample schema; solve ten of the interview problems without hints; reproduce the NOT IN with NULL bug
Storage and pages; Indexes; Reading query plans; The query planner; Query optimisation; Slow query diagnosis
Generate one million rows; compare Seq Scan, Index Scan and Bitmap Scan; fix a function-on-column query; show an N+1 from Hibernate in the SQL log
Transactions and ACID; Isolation levels; MVCC; Locking; WAL and recovery; Transactions in Java and Spring
Reproduce a lost update and write skew with two psql sessions; cause and read a deadlock log; kill a postgres and watch recovery
Connections and pooling; Replication; Backup and PITR; Partitioning and sharding; Why NoSQL; Distributed data fundamentals; MongoDB model, CRUD, aggregation, indexes
Set up streaming replication; run a PITR restore; compute a quorum example; write five aggregation pipelines
MongoDB transactions, replication, sharding, storage and operations; Spring Data MongoDB; Relational versus non-relational; Putting it together
Run the JSONB benchmark; write the Spring order service; run mock interviews on the whole bank
blocks.caption: Weekly plan mapped to chapters by name.

blocks.text:
### Method

1. Read a chapter once at normal speed, then close it and write the mechanism from memory in five lines; compare with the text.
2. Run every lab; change one parameter and predict the result before running again.
3. At the end of each day answer three questions from the bank aloud, then check the model answers; repeat the failures two days later.
4. In the last two days of week 6 give each scenario question as a procedure: observe (which tool), narrow (which query or plan), fix (immediate and permanent) and prevent.
5. Keep a one-page error log of every wrong answer with the correct mechanism; review it before each mock interview.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A plan works only when each week ends with a checkpoint that is answered without notes.

- Labs convert knowledge into evidence: run them, vary them, predict the result.
- Revisit weak questions after two days and again after a week.
- Treat scenario questions as diagnosis procedures with commands, not as definitions.

sections.title: Putting It Together: One Order Through the Whole Data Layer

blocks.text:
### Layer

The preceding chapters examined components separately. This chapter follows one request, `POST /orders`, from the HTTP layer to every system that stores a trace of it: the connection pool, the PostgreSQL transaction, the index structures, the write-ahead log, the replica, the cache and the MongoDB event log. The PostgreSQL part is a real trace obtained on the build machine; the Spring, Redis and MongoDB parts follow the documented behaviour and are labelled as such. The goal is that the reader can say, for any statement in the request, which structure it touches and what fails if that structure is slow or unavailable.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The request path

The design is the common one for a Java service: the relational database is the system of record and the other stores are derived from it.

1. **Spring Boot receives the request.** The controller validates the body and calls a service method annotated `@Transactional`. The proxy asks the transaction manager to begin a transaction.
2. **The pool lends a connection.** HikariCP returns an idle connection in microseconds, or waits up to `connectionTimeout` when all are in use. The connection is bound to the thread until the method ends, so everything done in the method is one database transaction.
3. **PostgreSQL executes the statements.** `INSERT INTO orders`, two `INSERT INTO order_items` and an `UPDATE` `stock`. Each statement searches indexes (B-tree descents), checks foreign keys (row locks on the referenced customer and products) and writes new tuple versions to heap pages in shared buffers.
4. **The WAL records the changes.** Every page modification generates a WAL record before the page may be written. At `COMMIT` the commit record is appended and the log is flushed to disk (`fsync`) before the client receives the acknowledgement.
5. **The replica replays the WAL.** A walsender streams the records to the standby, which replays them; reads from the replica are behind by the replication lag.
6. **The cache is invalidated.** The service deletes the cache key of the affected product's stock so that the next read reloads it (cache-aside).
7. **An event is written to MongoDB.** The order event is stored in the document store for history and analytics, written with `w: "majority"` and keyed by the outbox id so that a repeated delivery is harmless.
